answers.alternative_b: Yes, for specialised tools such as cloud storage and password management. I prefer paying for a trustworthy service rather than becoming the product through excessive data collection.

questions.question: What kind of app would you like someone to invent?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: I would love an app that combines all my teaching schedules, student notes and material versions without becoming complicated. At present, the information lives in several places, and finding one detail can feel like a small investigation.
answers.alternative_a: I want an app that shows how crowded a cafe or study space is in real time. It would save me travelling across the city only to discover that every seat is taken.
answers.alternative_b: I would invent a truly reliable app that predicts when household appliances are likely to fail. A warning before the refrigerator stops working would be far more useful than another social platform.

questions.question: Have apps changed the way you organize your life?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Absolutely. My calendar tells me where to be, my notes app captures ideas and reminders stop small tasks from disappearing. I am more organised now, although I may also be less capable of remembering anything without a notification.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially for group projects. Shared documents and planning apps make coordination much easier, though they also mean nobody can honestly claim they missed the latest update.
answers.alternative_b: They have made life more systematic. Bills, workouts and appointments are tracked automatically, which reduces mental clutter, but I still keep a paper list for the day's most important tasks.

questions.question: Do you like taking photos?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I do, but mainly to preserve ordinary family moments rather than create artistic images. A spontaneous photo of my children laughing often means more to me later than a perfectly arranged picture at a landmark.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, photography is one of my main hobbies. I like noticing light, colour and small details that most people walk past, and the camera gives me a reason to explore the city more slowly.
answers.alternative_b: I take photos occasionally, mostly while travelling or hiking. I am not interested in documenting every meal, but I like keeping a visual record of places that felt special.

questions.question: What do you usually photograph?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: Mostly my family, food and views from trips. I also photograph teaching notes or book pages, which is far less beautiful but probably the most practical use of my camera.
answers.alternative_a: I photograph street scenes, cafes and friends. I am drawn to ordinary moments with interesting light rather than formal poses.
answers.alternative_b: Landscapes are my favourite, especially the sea and mountains around Da Nang. I enjoy images that capture scale and quietness more than crowded portraits.

questions.question: Do you prefer taking photos or being in them?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I prefer taking photos because I feel slightly awkward posing. Behind the camera, I can focus on other people and the scene instead of wondering what to do with my hands.
answers.alternative_a: I enjoy both, although I am usually the photographer in my friend group. I have started asking others to take pictures of me too, or I end up absent from my own memories.
answers.alternative_b: Taking them, definitely. I like controlling the frame and timing, whereas being photographed makes me overthink my expression.

questions.question: How do you store your photographs?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Everything is backed up automatically to cloud storage, and I organise important albums by year and event. The system is not perfect, but it prevents thousands of images from becoming one endless, unsearchable stream.
answers.alternative_a: I keep them in cloud albums and print a small selection each year. Physical photos feel more meaningful because they are chosen rather than merely accumulated.
answers.alternative_b: I store originals on an external drive and copies online. It sounds overly cautious until someone loses a phone containing five years of photographs.

questions.question: Is there a photo that is especially important to you?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: There is one photo of my family on the rooftop shortly after we moved into our house. The image itself is not technically impressive, but it captures a moment when the place still felt new and full of possibility.
answers.alternative_a: A photograph of my grandmother holding my hand at graduation is especially important. She looked prouder than I felt, and the picture preserves an expression I never want to forget.
answers.alternative_b: I value a photo from my first solo mountain trip. I was exhausted and badly dressed, but it reminds me that I was capable of doing something that had genuinely frightened me.

questions.question: Are you interested in art?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I am interested in art, although I am more of an appreciative viewer than a knowledgeable one. I enjoy work that creates an immediate feeling or makes me notice an ordinary subject differently, even if I cannot explain the technique behind it.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially illustration and photography. I like seeing how different artists turn familiar streets or faces into something personal, and it often gives me ideas for my own creative projects.
answers.alternative_b: A little. I do not follow the art world closely, but I enjoy well-designed buildings, posters and digital art. I probably respond more to visual clarity than to abstract symbolism.

questions.question: Did you enjoy art lessons at school?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Not especially. I liked the freedom of the lessons, but my hands rarely produced what my mind imagined, which was frustrating. I was much happier discussing a picture than trying to draw one accurately.
answers.alternative_a: I loved them because they were a break from memorising facts. Even when my work was messy, the class gave me permission to experiment without one correct answer.
answers.alternative_b: I found them relaxing but was never particularly talented. My favourite activities were technical ones like perspective drawing because they gave me rules to follow.

questions.question: What kind of art do you like?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: I am drawn to landscape paintings and contemporary photography. Both can turn a familiar place into something worth looking at again, and I especially like images with strong natural light and a quiet atmosphere.
answers.alternative_a: I like colourful modern illustration, especially work used in books, posters and animation. It feels accessible and playful rather than intimidating.
answers.alternative_b: Minimalist digital art appeals to me. I like clean lines and limited detail because the artist has to communicate an idea without relying on visual clutter.

questions.question: Do you have any artwork in your home?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, we have a few framed photographs and one painting of a coastal village in central Vietnam. It is not a valuable piece, but the colours remind me of my hometown and make the living room feel more personal.
answers.alternative_a: My room has several small prints from local artists. I chose them slowly, so each one is connected to a place, exhibition or friend rather than being random decoration.
answers.alternative_b: Only one piece, a black-and-white city photograph above my desk. I prefer a simple room, and that image adds character without making the space feel busy.

questions.question: Would you like to learn to draw or paint?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: I would like to learn sketching, mainly so I could keep a visual travel journal. I do not expect to become an artist, but being able to capture a street or building in a few lines seems more personal than taking another phone photo.
answers.alternative_a: I would love to learn watercolour painting. The colours look soft and expressive, and the slight unpredictability of the paint seems part of the charm.
answers.alternative_b: I would try digital drawing because mistakes are easier to undo and the tools fit naturally with my technical background. Traditional paint feels less forgiving.

questions.question: Do you often visit museums or galleries?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not regularly, perhaps a few times a year. I tend to visit when travelling because museums give context to a place, but I rarely wake up on an ordinary weekend and decide to spend the afternoon in one.
answers.alternative_a: Quite often, especially when a gallery has a temporary exhibition. Student discounts make visits affordable, and they are a pleasant alternative to meeting friends in another cafe.
answers.alternative_b: Occasionally. I enjoy museums, but I need a specific reason to go, such as a technology exhibition or a visiting collection, rather than wandering through every room.

questions.question: What kind of museum interests you most?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: History museums interest me most, particularly those that use personal stories and everyday objects. A soldier's letter or an old household item can make a period feel more real than a wall full of dates.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer art and design museums. I like exhibitions that show the process behind a piece, because seeing sketches and failed ideas makes creativity feel less mysterious.
answers.alternative_b: Science and technology museums are my favourite. Interactive displays help me understand difficult ideas, and I can spend far too long pressing buttons meant for children.

questions.question: Did you visit museums as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, mainly on school trips. At the time, I was more interested in talking to friends than reading labels, but some of the large exhibits stayed in my memory and made later history lessons easier to imagine.
answers.alternative_a: My parents took me to museums whenever we travelled. I did not appreciate every visit, but the habit made cultural places feel normal rather than formal or intimidating.
answers.alternative_b: Only rarely. My hometown did not have many museums, so most of my childhood exposure came from books and television documentaries.

questions.question: What makes a museum enjoyable?
questions.quick_analysis: Identify the key factor or solution, explain how it works, and illustrate it with one practical consequence.

answers.ta_refined: A clear story makes the biggest difference. I enjoy museums that guide visitors through a question or period rather than presenting hundreds of unrelated objects. Good lighting, short explanations and places to sit also matter more than institutions sometimes realise.
answers.alternative_a: Interactive elements make a museum enjoyable for me. Being able to listen, touch or try something turns the visit into an experience rather than a long walk past glass cases.
answers.alternative_b: I value depth without overload. A smaller exhibition with carefully chosen items and strong explanations is far more memorable than an enormous collection that leaves me exhausted.

questions.question: Should museums be free to enter?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Basic national museums should probably be free or very inexpensive because they preserve shared history and education. Special exhibitions could still charge admission, since borrowing major collections and maintaining them costs real money.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, at least for students and children. Removing the price barrier would encourage people to visit casually, not only when a school organises the trip.
answers.alternative_b: Not necessarily. A reasonable ticket price can support preservation and better displays. I would rather pay a little for a well-maintained museum than enter a neglected one for free.

questions.question: Do you pay attention to advertisements?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Only when an advertisement is unusually relevant or irritating. Most of them blend into the background because I have learned to scroll past automatically, but a clear message or clever piece of humour can still catch my attention.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, probably more than I should. I am interested in marketing, so I often notice the colour, wording and target audience even when I have no intention of buying the product.
answers.alternative_b: Not much. I use ad blockers where possible and ignore most sponsored posts. I pay attention only when I am already comparing a product or service.

questions.question: Where do you usually see advertising?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: Mostly on social media and video platforms. I still see billboards during my commute, but online advertising follows my interests so closely that it is much harder to miss.
answers.alternative_a: Instagram, TikTok and outdoor screens around shopping centres are the main places. Advertising now feels woven into entertainment rather than separated from it.
answers.alternative_b: I see it mainly on websites, streaming services and inside free apps. The most noticeable ads are often the ones interrupting something I was trying to do.

questions.question: Have you ever bought something because of an advertisement?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, an advertisement once persuaded me to try a language-learning subscription. The demonstration was clear and addressed a problem I actually had. I stayed because the product was useful, but the ad definitely opened the door.
answers.alternative_a: I bought a skincare product after seeing several short videos about it. The packaging and reviews looked convincing, although the result was much less dramatic than the advertisement suggested.
answers.alternative_b: I purchased noise-cancelling headphones after watching a detailed comparison. It was partly advertising, but the technical evidence was strong enough to influence my decision.

questions.question: What kind of advertising annoys you?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: Repeated ads are the worst, especially when I have already bought the product. Seeing the same message twenty times makes the company feel intrusive rather than memorable.
answers.alternative_a: I dislike advertisements that pretend to be ordinary personal recommendations. When sponsorship is hidden, the viewer is being manipulated rather than informed.
answers.alternative_b: Loud, unskippable video ads annoy me most. The sudden change in volume feels designed to punish the audience into paying attention.

questions.question: Do you think advertisements influence children?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Absolutely. Children may not recognise persuasive techniques, so they can treat exaggerated claims as facts. Bright colours, games and popular characters make the influence even stronger because the advertising feels like entertainment.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially with food, toys and fashion. Children often want what their friends have seen online, and repeated exposure can turn a passing interest into a demand.
answers.alternative_b: They do, although parents and schools can reduce the effect by teaching media literacy. Banning every advertisement is unrealistic; helping children question them is more sustainable.

questions.question: How do you usually get the news?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I usually check a few trusted news websites in the morning and listen to short audio updates while travelling. I avoid relying on a single source because the choice of headline can shape a story almost as much as the facts.
answers.alternative_a: Most news reaches me through mobile notifications and social media, and then I open a reliable article if the story matters. It is quick, although I have to be careful not to confuse popularity with accuracy.
answers.alternative_b: I use news apps and a daily email summary. The email is useful because it gives me a broad overview without inviting endless scrolling.

questions.question: What kinds of news interest you?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: I follow education, technology and major economic developments most closely because they affect my work and family decisions. I also pay attention to national news, but I try not to consume every breaking update when the facts are still unclear.
answers.alternative_a: I am interested in culture, environmental issues and stories about young people. Political news matters, but I prefer explainers to constant conflict-driven headlines.
answers.alternative_b: Technology, science and business news are my main interests. I enjoy understanding how a new invention or policy might change ordinary life rather than simply knowing that it happened.

questions.question: Do you prefer reading or watching the news?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Reading, because I can control the pace, compare sources and return to a specific sentence. Video can be engaging, but dramatic music and images sometimes create a stronger emotional reaction than the evidence deserves.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer watching a short news programme for the main stories and then reading about anything complicated. The combination gives me both speed and detail.
answers.alternative_b: Reading, without question. It is faster, quieter and easier to verify, especially when a technical story includes figures or links to original research.

questions.question: How often do you discuss news with other people?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: A few times a week, usually with my wife or colleagues when a story affects education, prices or family life. I do not enjoy arguing for sport, so the discussion has to lead somewhere useful.
answers.alternative_a: Almost every day. My classmates share stories in group chats, and news often becomes the starting point for a larger conversation about society or careers.
answers.alternative_b: Not very often. I discuss major events with close friends, but I avoid long online debates because they usually generate heat rather than understanding.

questions.question: Do you think social media is a reliable news source?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: It can be a useful alert system, but not a reliable final source. Posts spread quickly and show what people are discussing, yet I still need to check the original report and the date before believing or sharing anything.
answers.alternative_a: Not by itself. Social media gives access to many viewpoints, but algorithms reward emotional content, so misleading stories can appear more credible simply because they are repeated.
answers.alternative_b: It depends on the account. Official organisations and qualified experts can be valuable, but anonymous screenshots and clipped videos should be treated as leads to verify, not evidence.

questions.question: Do you write much by hand?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not much beyond quick notes and the occasional card. Most of my work is digital because I revise materials constantly, and typing makes changes painless. My handwriting now appears mainly when technology would be slower than a pen.
answers.alternative_a: Quite a lot. I take lecture notes by hand because the physical act helps me remember ideas, even though my notebooks become increasingly chaotic near exams.
answers.alternative_b: Very little. I type almost everything at work and use my phone for personal lists. When I do write a long paragraph, my hand tires embarrassingly quickly.

questions.question: What do you usually write?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I write lesson plans, short reminders and comments on student work. I also keep a small notebook for ideas because opening a phone can lead me into three unrelated apps before I remember why I picked it up.
answers.alternative_a: Mostly class notes, to-do lists and journal entries. Writing by hand makes private thoughts feel slower and more deliberate.
answers.alternative_b: I write signatures, labels and the occasional diagram. Technical ideas are sometimes easier to sketch on paper before turning them into code.

questions.question: Do you prefer typing or handwriting?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Typing for anything long, handwriting for thinking. A keyboard is faster and easier to edit, but a pen helps me focus when I am planning an argument or trying to untangle an idea.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer handwriting for studying because I remember more, although typing is better for assignments. Each method solves a different problem.
answers.alternative_b: Typing, definitely. My work depends on speed, search and version control, none of which paper handles well. I still sketch rough diagrams by hand.

questions.question: Has your handwriting changed over time?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: It has become less neat because I use it less often and write faster when I do. At school, teachers cared about presentation; now my notes only need to be understood by one increasingly forgiving reader - me.
answers.alternative_a: It has become smaller and more personal. I used to copy textbook-style letters, whereas now I write quickly and connect most of them, which looks messier but feels more natural.
answers.alternative_b: My handwriting has deteriorated. Years of typing have made it stiff and uneven, so filling out a long form feels like an unexpected physical challenge.

questions.question: Do you think handwriting will remain important?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, but in a narrower role. People will still need to sign documents, make quick notes and develop basic motor skills, even if most professional communication remains digital. It may become less common without becoming irrelevant.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. Handwriting is useful for memory, creativity and personal communication. A handwritten note also carries more emotional weight precisely because it takes extra effort.
answers.alternative_b: It will remain useful, but not central. Schools should teach it clearly, then spend more time on digital literacy once students can write comfortably.

questions.question: Do you send many emails?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I send several emails each day for work, mainly about schedules, materials and feedback. Email is still useful when a message needs structure or a record, although for simple questions it can feel unnecessarily formal.
answers.alternative_a: Not many personal emails, but plenty for university and job applications. Most everyday conversations happen through messaging apps, so email now signals that something is official.
answers.alternative_b: I send emails regularly at work, especially for technical decisions and project summaries. For quick updates, my team uses chat because an email thread can become heavy very quickly.

questions.question: Who do you usually message during the day?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: I message my wife, students and a few work groups throughout the day. The messages range from important scheduling changes to extremely urgent questions about what we are having for dinner.
answers.alternative_a: Mostly classmates, close friends and my sister. University group chats are especially active because somebody is always asking about a deadline that was announced clearly.
answers.alternative_b: I mainly message colleagues and family. Work chats are practical and brief; family messages are usually photos, reminders or links someone insists I must see.

questions.question: Do you prefer calling or texting?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Texting for routine communication, calling when the issue is emotional or complicated. A three-minute conversation can prevent twenty confusing messages, but I dislike receiving unexpected calls with no warning.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer texting because it gives me time to think and reply when convenient. I call close family members, but with friends, messages feel more natural.
answers.alternative_b: Calling is better for decisions that need quick clarification. Text is useful for records, but tone is easy to misread when a discussion becomes sensitive.

questions.question: Have messaging apps changed the way you communicate?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Completely. Communication is faster, more visual and much more continuous. The downside is that people can feel permanently available, so a delayed reply is sometimes treated as a statement rather than simply a busy day.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, group chats have made planning far easier. At the same time, they create an endless stream of minor updates, and important information can disappear under jokes and stickers.
answers.alternative_b: They have reduced formal barriers at work. I can ask a colleague a small question instantly, but the constant flow also fragments concentration if notifications are not controlled.

questions.question: Is it important to reply to messages quickly?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: It depends on urgency. Work messages and practical questions deserve a reasonably quick reply, but nobody should expect an immediate response to every casual comment. Fast communication should not mean permanent obligation.
answers.alternative_a: Generally yes, because silence can delay other people's plans. I try to acknowledge important messages even when I cannot give a full answer yet.
answers.alternative_b: No, not automatically. A thoughtful reply later is often better than a rushed one now. The sender should make urgency clear instead of assuming everyone is watching their phone.

questions.question: What languages can you speak?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: Vietnamese is my first language, and I speak English confidently for work. I also know a little Mandarin, although at the moment it is enough for greetings and ordering food rather than a serious conversation.
answers.alternative_a: I speak Vietnamese and English, and I have studied some Korean through online lessons. My Korean is still basic, but I can understand familiar expressions in songs and dramas.
answers.alternative_b: I speak Vietnamese and English. I can read a small amount of Japanese because of my interest in technology, but speaking it is another matter entirely.

questions.question: Why are you learning English?
questions.quick_analysis: Give the main reason directly, explain the cause-and-effect link, and finish with a brief personal consequence.

answers.ta_refined: English gives me access to a much wider professional and intellectual world. It allows me to teach, read research directly and communicate with people beyond Vietnam, so for me it is both a career tool and a source of independence.
answers.alternative_a: I am learning it because it is essential for my degree and future career. More personally, I want to travel without depending on translation apps for every small interaction.
answers.alternative_b: Most technical documentation is written in English, so the language is unavoidable in software. It also lets me work with international teams and understand ideas before they are translated.

questions.question: Which part of English do you find most difficult?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: Natural speaking is the hardest part. I can plan accurate sentences, but real conversation requires instant choices, listening and adjustment. The challenge is not knowing more grammar; it is using what I know without sounding like I am assembling a puzzle.
answers.alternative_a: Pronunciation is most difficult for me, especially ending sounds and word stress. I can know exactly what I want to say and still feel that the sound does not match the version in my head.
answers.alternative_b: Idiomatic listening is challenging. Native speakers reduce sounds, change pace and use references that textbooks rarely explain, so understanding informal conversation takes constant exposure.

questions.question: How do you practice speaking?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I practise by teaching, recording model answers and discussing topics aloud rather than only reading them. Listening back is uncomfortable but useful because it exposes repeated phrases and unnatural pauses that I do not notice in the moment.
answers.alternative_a: I join an English club, shadow short videos and send voice messages to friends. The variety keeps practice from feeling like another formal class.
answers.alternative_b: I speak during online technical meetings and explain concepts aloud to myself. Teaching a solution, even to an empty room, quickly reveals where my language or thinking is unclear.

questions.question: What other language would you like to learn?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I would like to learn Mandarin properly because it would be useful in Asia and open access to a huge culture and business environment. The writing system looks demanding, but that difficulty is also part of what attracts me.
answers.alternative_a: I would choose Spanish. It is spoken in many countries, sounds energetic and would make travel across several regions much easier.
answers.alternative_b: Japanese interests me because of technology, design and literature. I already recognise a few words, so building that into real communication would be satisfying.

questions.question: Do you use a dictionary?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, constantly, but almost always online. I use dictionaries to check pronunciation, collocations and example sentences rather than only meanings, because knowing what a word means does not guarantee that I can use it naturally.
answers.alternative_a: I use one several times a week for university reading. I usually check a word quickly, save it and then forget half of the saved list, so I am trying to review more systematically.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, mainly for precise technical or English terms. A dictionary is useful when a rough translation would hide an important distinction.

questions.question: Do you prefer online or printed dictionaries?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Online dictionaries, without question. They are faster, searchable and include audio, usage labels and large collections of examples. Printed dictionaries are beautiful objects, but carrying one is difficult to justify now.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer online versions because I can use them on my phone during class or travel. I still keep an old printed dictionary because it reminds me of school.
answers.alternative_b: Online. I need current terminology and quick cross-references, and digital tools make comparison between several sources almost effortless.

questions.question: What information do you look for in a dictionary?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Pronunciation and collocation come first. I want to know which preposition, verb or noun naturally sits beside a word. I also check whether an expression is formal, informal or uncommon, since register can change an answer completely.
answers.alternative_a: I look for a simple definition, a few examples and the word family. Seeing the adjective, noun and verb together helps me use the vocabulary flexibly.
answers.alternative_b: I focus on exact meaning, usage notes and domain labels. In technical writing, two words that look like synonyms may carry different assumptions.

questions.question: Did your teachers encourage you to use dictionaries?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, particularly in secondary school. My teachers taught us to look up unfamiliar words instead of immediately asking for a translation, which made us more independent and occasionally sent us down interesting vocabulary rabbit holes.
answers.alternative_a: They did, although the classroom dictionaries were shared and slightly outdated. We still learned the valuable habit of checking rather than guessing.
answers.alternative_b: Some teachers encouraged it, but most vocabulary was given through lists. I developed stronger dictionary habits later when I needed accuracy for university and work.

questions.question: Do you think translation apps can replace dictionaries?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Not completely. Translation apps are excellent for speed and context, but dictionaries explain pronunciation, grammar, register and patterns of use. A translation can tell me the destination; a good dictionary shows the road.
answers.alternative_a: They can replace dictionaries for simple travel needs, but not for serious language learning. Automatic translations often hide why one phrase sounds natural and another does not.
answers.alternative_b: No. Translation tools predict an equivalent in context, whereas dictionaries let users examine meanings and make informed choices. The two tools complement each other.

questions.question: Did you enjoy mathematics at school?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I enjoyed it because answers felt clear and earned. A difficult problem could be broken into steps, and reaching the correct result gave me a sense of control that more interpretive subjects did not always provide.
answers.alternative_a: I liked mathematics until the problems became highly abstract. Basic algebra was satisfying, but once symbols seemed disconnected from real situations, my confidence dropped.
answers.alternative_b: Very much. I enjoyed patterns and logical puzzles, and mathematics eventually helped lead me towards programming.

questions.question: Are you good at doing calculations in your head?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Reasonably good with everyday calculations, especially percentages and rough estimates. I am not a human calculator, but I can usually tell when a price, bill or answer is obviously wrong before reaching for a device.
answers.alternative_a: Only with simple numbers. I can split a restaurant bill, but if someone watches me calculate, even basic arithmetic suddenly becomes a public performance.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, particularly with binary-style thinking, proportions and estimates. For precise large numbers, I still use a calculator because confidence is not the same as accuracy.

questions.question: When do you use mathematics in daily life?
questions.quick_analysis: Anchor the answer in a clear time, add one vivid detail, and connect the memory to how you see it now.

answers.ta_refined: I use it when budgeting, comparing discounts, measuring spaces and interpreting student results. Much of it is simple, but numerical sense helps me make quicker decisions and question figures that seem suspicious.
answers.alternative_a: I use it for shopping, cooking and planning travel costs. University statistics also appears more often in marketing than I expected.
answers.alternative_b: It is part of my work through algorithms, performance estimates and data analysis. Outside work, I use it for finances and fitness tracking.

questions.question: Do you ever use a calculator?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Of course. I use one whenever precision matters or the calculation has several steps. Refusing a calculator for the sake of pride would be an odd way to turn a small task into a large mistake.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, mostly on my phone. I use it for percentages, currency conversion and checking group expenses before someone pays the wrong amount.
answers.alternative_b: Frequently at work. Calculators and scripts reduce careless errors, while mental estimates help me judge whether the output is sensible.

questions.question: Why do some people find mathematics difficult?
questions.quick_analysis: Give the main reason directly, explain the cause-and-effect link, and finish with a brief personal consequence.

answers.ta_refined: Many people meet mathematics as a set of rules before they understand what the rules represent. Once they fall behind, each new topic rests on a weak foundation, so anxiety grows alongside the difficulty.
answers.alternative_a: It is often taught too quickly and with one approved method. Students who need a visual or practical explanation may conclude that they lack ability when they actually need a different route.
answers.alternative_b: Mathematics is cumulative and unforgiving of gaps. A small misunderstanding in fractions can return years later inside algebra or statistics, making the later topic seem harder than it truly is.

questions.question: Did you enjoy learning history at school?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, especially when lessons focused on people and consequences rather than memorising dates. History made the present feel less accidental, although I admit that long lists of battles and rulers could still drain the life out of it.
answers.alternative_a: I enjoyed social and cultural history more than political chronology. Learning how ordinary people lived made the past feel human instead of distant.
answers.alternative_b: I liked it moderately. The broad patterns were fascinating, but I struggled when assessment rewarded exact recall more than understanding.

questions.question: Which period of history interests you most?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: Vietnam's twentieth-century history interests me most because its effects are still visible in families, cities and national identity. It is close enough to feel personal, yet complex enough that one simple story is never sufficient.
answers.alternative_a: I am fascinated by ancient civilisations, particularly Egypt and Greece. Their architecture and myths are familiar, but the everyday societies behind them still feel mysterious.
answers.alternative_b: The industrial revolution interests me because it connects technology, labour and urban life. Many modern systems began there, including some of the problems we still debate.

questions.question: How do you usually learn about the past?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I read books and long articles, but documentaries are often my entry point. A strong visual overview gives me a map of the period, and then I can investigate details without getting lost.
answers.alternative_a: Museums, podcasts and historical novels all help me. I know novels are not evidence, but they can create curiosity that leads me towards reliable sources.
answers.alternative_b: I prefer lectures and primary documents. Hearing an expert explain the context and then reading original letters or reports makes the period feel both structured and immediate.

questions.question: Is there a historical figure you admire?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I admire Ho Chi Minh for his historical role, but I am also interested in educators such as Chu Van An, whose commitment to integrity has remained meaningful across centuries. I tend to respect figures whose influence extended beyond personal power.
answers.alternative_a: I admire Marie Curie because her scientific work required extraordinary discipline, and she succeeded in an environment that offered women very little space.
answers.alternative_b: Alan Turing is a figure I admire. His intellectual contribution was enormous, and the injustice he faced is a reminder that societies can depend on people while still failing them.

questions.question: Should children visit historical places?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Definitely. A historical site turns abstract information into physical scale and atmosphere. Standing inside an old prison, temple or battlefield can create questions that a textbook never triggers, provided the visit is prepared rather than treated as a day off.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, because children remember places and stories more easily than lists. A visit can also help them connect national history with their own community.
answers.alternative_b: They should, but the trip needs guidance. Without a clear task or engaging explanation, students may simply take photographs and leave without understanding what they saw.

questions.question: What is your favorite color?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: Dark blue is probably my favourite. It looks calm, professional and easy to combine with almost anything, so choosing clothes becomes one less decision in the morning. It is not an adventurous preference, but it has served me well.
answers.alternative_a: I love green, especially soft sage green. It reminds me of plants and quiet spaces, and it can make even a small room feel fresher.
answers.alternative_b: Black is my favourite because it is simple and practical. It works for clothes, devices and furniture, and it hides the fact that I am not very imaginative with colour.

questions.question: Are there any colors you dislike?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I am not keen on very bright neon colours. They can work in small details, but a whole outfit in fluorescent yellow feels more like a safety warning than a fashion choice.
answers.alternative_a: I dislike muddy brown because it can make clothes and rooms look tired. I would not ban it entirely, but I rarely choose it voluntarily.
answers.alternative_b: I avoid vivid orange. It attracts too much attention for my taste, although it looks great on other people who can carry it confidently.

questions.question: Do colors affect your mood?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, more than I used to realise. Cool colours and natural tones help me relax, whereas overly bright rooms can feel tiring after a while. I would not call it magic, but colour definitely shapes atmosphere.
answers.alternative_a: Absolutely. Wearing a bright colour can lift my mood on a grey day, and a dark, cluttered room can make me feel less energetic.
answers.alternative_b: A little. I prefer neutral surroundings when I need to concentrate, but colour has less influence on me than noise or lighting.

questions.question: What colors do you usually wear?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Mostly navy, white, grey and black. Those colours are easy to mix and appropriate for teaching, so I can get dressed quickly without creating an accidental costume.
answers.alternative_a: I wear a lot of cream, blue and pastel colours. They suit my style and look good in photographs without being too loud.
answers.alternative_b: My wardrobe is mainly black, grey and olive green. I value practicality, and these colours survive repeated use without looking dated.

questions.question: Has your favorite color changed since childhood?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes. As a child, I loved red because it felt bold and energetic. Over time, I moved towards darker blues and neutral colours, perhaps because adulthood involves fewer opportunities to dress like a superhero.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. I used to insist that pink was childish, but now I enjoy softer pink shades. Taste becomes less defensive as people grow more confident.
answers.alternative_b: Not much. I liked black and blue even as a teenager, although I now combine them more carefully instead of wearing the darkest item available.

questions.question: What sports do you enjoy?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I enjoy badminton and basketball, although these days I play less regularly than I would like. Both are fast enough to keep me engaged, and they turn exercise into a game rather than a negotiation with myself.
answers.alternative_a: I love volleyball and swimming. Volleyball gives me the energy of a team, while swimming is the activity I choose when I need a quieter form of exercise.
answers.alternative_b: I enjoy football, badminton and hiking. I am not highly competitive, but I like sports that require movement, timing and a little strategy.

questions.question: How often do you play or watch sports?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: I exercise three times a week, but I watch sport only when there is a major tournament or an important match. Following every league would require a second full-time job.
answers.alternative_a: I play volleyball once or twice a week and watch highlights online. I rarely sit through an entire match unless friends are watching too.
answers.alternative_b: I play badminton at weekends and follow football fairly closely. Watching is easier to fit into a busy week, although playing is obviously better for my health.

questions.question: Did you play sports at school?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, mainly football and badminton. School competitions were quite serious, and even students who claimed not to care became intensely patriotic about their class once a match began.
answers.alternative_a: I played volleyball for my school team. I was never the star player, but the training taught me discipline and gave me a strong group of friends.
answers.alternative_b: I played football during breaks and took formal swimming lessons. The football was chaotic, but it is probably where I learned to cooperate with very little discussion.

questions.question: Do you prefer team or individual sports?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Individual sports suit my schedule better because I can exercise whenever I am free. Team sports are more exciting, though, and I miss the sense of shared purpose when everyone is working towards the same result.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer team sports. The social atmosphere keeps me motivated, and I work harder when other people are depending on me.
answers.alternative_b: Individual sports, by a small margin. I like controlling the pace and measuring progress against my previous performance rather than another person's.

questions.question: Is there a sport you would like to learn?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I would like to learn tennis. It combines fitness, technique and strategy, and it is a sport I could continue playing for many years. The main obstacle is finding enough time and a patient partner.
answers.alternative_a: I want to try surfing. It looks difficult, but the mixture of balance, sea and speed is exactly what makes it appealing.
answers.alternative_b: I would like to learn archery. It seems calm and precise, which is a refreshing contrast to noisy team sports.

questions.question: How do you keep physically active?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I alternate between running and weight training three times a week. That combination covers both cardio and strength without requiring me to live at the gym. The diet side is still a work in progress, because knowing what to do and doing it are different skills.
answers.alternative_a: I walk everywhere I can, attend a dance class and do short home workouts. Variety helps because I lose motivation quickly if exercise becomes repetitive.
answers.alternative_b: I go to the gym after work and play badminton at weekends. I also take the stairs whenever possible, although I will not pretend that makes me an athlete.

questions.question: How often do you exercise?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: Usually three sessions a week. I aim for consistency rather than heroic effort, because an intense plan that lasts ten days is less useful than a moderate routine I can maintain for months.
answers.alternative_a: Four or five times a week, but some sessions are only twenty minutes. Short workouts are easier to fit around university and still make a difference.
answers.alternative_b: Three times weekly, plus casual walking. I schedule exercise like a meeting; otherwise, work expands and quietly takes the time.

questions.question: Do you prefer exercising indoors or outdoors?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Indoors, mainly because the weather in Ho Chi Minh City can be brutally hot or suddenly wet. A treadmill is less inspiring than a park, but air conditioning makes consistency much easier.
answers.alternative_a: Outdoors. I enjoy the changing scenery and feel less conscious of time when I run around a lake rather than stare at a gym wall.
answers.alternative_b: I prefer indoors for strength training and outdoors for walking or cycling. The best environment depends on the activity rather than one general preference.

questions.question: What stops people from exercising regularly?
questions.quick_analysis: Identify the key factor or solution, explain how it works, and illustrate it with one practical consequence.

answers.ta_refined: Time is the obvious barrier, but lack of routine is often the deeper one. If exercise depends on feeling motivated, it is easy to postpone. A fixed schedule removes some of that daily argument.
answers.alternative_a: People often start with goals that are too ambitious. When the plan becomes painful or inconvenient, they assume they lack discipline instead of adjusting the plan.
answers.alternative_b: Work, family obligations and poor facilities can all interfere. Some people also dislike exercise because their only experience was competitive school sport rather than an activity they personally enjoyed.

questions.question: Have your exercise habits changed?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, they have become more structured. I used to exercise in bursts whenever I felt guilty, whereas now I follow a simple weekly plan. It is less dramatic but far more effective.
answers.alternative_a: I am more active now than at school because I choose the activities myself. Exercise stopped feeling like a compulsory class and became a way to manage stress.
answers.alternative_b: My routine has shifted from team sport to gym-based exercise. It is not as social, but it fits adult schedules and allows me to train even when friends are unavailable.

questions.question: Do you walk much during a normal day?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not as much as I should. I walk around my neighbourhood and between nearby appointments, but motorbike travel still dominates my day. I sometimes check my step count in the evening and discover that my phone has been more mobile than I have.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, quite a lot. I walk across campus, to the bus stop and around shopping areas, so I usually reach a reasonable number of steps without planning a workout.
answers.alternative_b: I walk during lunch and after dinner, but work itself is very sedentary. On weekdays, those short walks are important because otherwise I could spend hours moving only my fingers.

questions.question: Where do you enjoy going for a walk?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: I enjoy walking along the river or in a quiet park, preferably early in the morning. The air is cooler, the paths are less crowded and the city briefly feels more generous.
answers.alternative_a: My favourite place is the lake near my university. There are trees, food stalls and plenty of people, so it feels lively without being stressful.
answers.alternative_b: I like the coastal path in Da Nang. The view changes with the weather, and even a short walk there can clear my head after a difficult day.

questions.question: Did you walk more when you were younger?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, much more. I walked or cycled everywhere in my hometown because school, friends and shops were close together. In Ho Chi Minh City, distance and traffic have made walking less natural.
answers.alternative_a: Probably. As a child, I spent entire afternoons outside, whereas now many journeys are made by bus or motorbike for the sake of time.
answers.alternative_b: I walked more for play but less deliberately. Today I go for walks to exercise or think, while childhood movement happened without counting or planning.

questions.question: Do you prefer walking alone or with someone?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Alone when I need to think, with someone when the purpose is social. A solo walk helps me organise ideas, but walking with my wife often creates better conversation than sitting across a table.
answers.alternative_a: With a friend. Conversation makes the distance disappear, and walking side by side feels less formal than meeting for a serious talk.
answers.alternative_b: Usually alone. I like setting my own pace and listening to a podcast, although family walks at weekends are a pleasant exception.

questions.question: How could your city be made better for pedestrians?
questions.quick_analysis: Identify the key factor or solution, explain how it works, and illustrate it with one practical consequence.

answers.ta_refined: It needs continuous pavements, safer crossings and more shade. At present, pedestrians often compete with parked motorbikes, street stalls and turning traffic, so walking can feel like an obstacle course rather than transport.
answers.alternative_a: The city should widen pavements and enforce parking rules. A beautiful walkway is useless if every few metres people have to step into the road.
answers.alternative_b: More trees, pedestrian crossings and connected routes would help. People walk when the journey feels safe and direct, not merely because a campaign tells them it is healthy.

questions.question: Do you know how to ride a bicycle?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, although I am no longer a regular cyclist. I learned as a child on a bicycle that was slightly too large, so the first few lessons involved more courage than balance.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, and I still enjoy it. Cycling gives me a sense of independence because I can move quickly without waiting for transport or worrying about fuel.
answers.alternative_b: Of course. I learned early and later used a bicycle for school, exercise and short errands.

questions.question: How often do you cycle?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: Rarely in the city because traffic makes it stressful. I sometimes cycle during holidays or in quieter coastal areas, where I can enjoy the ride instead of constantly watching for motorbikes.
answers.alternative_a: Several times a week. I cycle to campus when the weather is pleasant, and it is often faster than taking a bus for short journeys.
answers.alternative_b: Usually at weekends. I ride along the coast or in less crowded areas for exercise rather than daily commuting.

questions.question: Did you ride a bike as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, almost every day. A bicycle was my main form of freedom, and my friends and I could disappear around the neighbourhood for hours as long as we returned before dark.
answers.alternative_a: I did. I rode to school and to my grandparents' house, and I remember decorating the basket with stickers that looked much better to me than to anyone else.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, extensively. My bicycle carried schoolbooks, footballs and occasionally another child, although the last use was neither safe nor approved.

questions.question: Is cycling safe where you live?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not particularly. Motorbikes and cars often pass too closely, and dedicated cycle lanes are rare or blocked. I can ride, but I would not feel comfortable letting a young child cycle alone.
answers.alternative_a: It is manageable around campus and parks but dangerous on major roads. The infrastructure changes abruptly, so a safe route can become stressful within one junction.
answers.alternative_b: Some coastal routes are good, but the city as a whole is inconsistent. Drivers are not always used to sharing space with bicycles.

questions.question: Would you use a bicycle more if there were better cycle lanes?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: Definitely. If there were protected lanes and secure parking, I would use a bicycle for short errands and exercise. At present, the health benefits do not always outweigh the traffic anxiety.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially for trips under five kilometres. Better lanes would save money and make cycling feel like ordinary transport rather than a risky hobby.
answers.alternative_b: I would. The distance is not the problem; safety and continuity are. A lane that ends suddenly at a busy intersection does not inspire confidence.

questions.question: Can you swim?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, well enough to be safe and comfortable in the water. I am not especially fast, but I can swim several lengths and do not panic if the water is deeper than expected.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, and it is one of my favourite forms of exercise. I enjoy the feeling of moving without impact on my joints.
answers.alternative_b: I can swim confidently. Living near the coast made it feel less like a sport and more like a basic life skill.

questions.question: How did you learn to swim?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I learned at a public pool when I was around ten. The instructor first taught us to float, which felt impossible until the moment I stopped fighting the water.
answers.alternative_a: My father taught me during summer holidays. His method was patient and gradual, which was fortunate because I was afraid of putting my face underwater.
answers.alternative_b: I learned in the sea with older cousins, although formal lessons later corrected several bad habits that enthusiasm had created.

questions.question: How often do you go swimming?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: Only a few times a month. I enjoy it, but reaching a pool and changing takes more time than a quick gym session, so swimming is usually a weekend activity.
answers.alternative_a: Once or twice a week when my schedule allows. It is both exercise and a mental break because phones and notifications cannot follow me into the pool.
answers.alternative_b: I swim mainly in summer or during coastal trips. I would do it more often if there were a convenient pool near my workplace.

questions.question: Do you prefer swimming in a pool or in the sea?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: A pool for exercise, the sea for experience. Pools are clean, measured and predictable, while the sea is more beautiful but comes with waves, currents and sand in places sand should never be.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer the sea because the space feels open and exciting. A pool is safer, but swimming repeated lengths can become monotonous.
answers.alternative_b: For serious swimming, a pool. For relaxing, the sea. I respect open water enough not to confuse scenic with harmless.

questions.question: Why is swimming a useful skill?
questions.quick_analysis: Give the main reason directly, explain the cause-and-effect link, and finish with a brief personal consequence.

answers.ta_refined: It can save a life, either your own or someone else's. It also makes travel and water activities far more enjoyable because fear does not control every decision near a pool, river or beach.
answers.alternative_a: Swimming provides safety, fitness and confidence. Children who learn early can participate in many activities without feeling excluded.
answers.alternative_b: It is useful because water is common and unpredictable. Even people who never swim competitively should know how to float, breathe and reach safety.

questions.question: Do you enjoy outdoor activities?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, especially activities that combine movement with scenery, such as hiking or cycling. Being outdoors helps me mentally detach from work in a way that an indoor workout often does not.
answers.alternative_a: Very much. I enjoy picnics, photography walks and outdoor sports because they turn exercise into a social experience.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, particularly hiking, swimming and camping. I like activities where the environment is part of the challenge rather than merely a background.

questions.question: What outdoor activity is popular where you live?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Jogging and badminton are extremely popular, especially in parks early in the morning. In the evening, public spaces fill with walkers, dance groups and children on scooters, so exercise becomes quite communal.
answers.alternative_a: People often walk around lakes, play football and take outdoor fitness classes. Social media has also made weekend hiking groups more common.
answers.alternative_b: Swimming and beach sports are popular in Da Nang, along with cycling along the coast. The landscape makes outdoor exercise an obvious choice.

questions.question: What did you like doing outdoors as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I rode bicycles, played football and explored any empty field that looked remotely suitable. We did not call it outdoor recreation; it was simply what happened once homework was finished.
answers.alternative_a: I loved skipping games, cycling and making pretend shops with friends outside our houses. The activities changed constantly because imagination supplied most of the equipment.
answers.alternative_b: I spent a lot of time swimming, climbing trees and playing football. Childhood safety standards were apparently more relaxed than they are now.

questions.question: Do you prefer active or relaxing outdoor activities?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Relaxing activities, by a small margin. A gentle walk or picnic allows me to enjoy the environment and conversation, whereas a very demanding activity can turn the scenery into something I barely notice.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer active ones like hiking or volleyball. I feel more refreshed after moving than after simply sitting outdoors.
answers.alternative_b: It depends on the week. After long hours at a desk, I want physical challenge; after a stressful period, a quiet walk near the sea is enough.

questions.question: Is there an outdoor activity you would like to try?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I would like to try kayaking. It offers exercise, a different view of the landscape and just enough adventure without requiring extreme courage or expensive training.
answers.alternative_a: I want to try paragliding. The idea is frightening, but seeing a city or coastline from the air would be unforgettable.
answers.alternative_b: Rock climbing outdoors appeals to me. I have tried indoor climbing, but real rock would add navigation, weather and a stronger sense of achievement.

questions.question: Do you often visit parks?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, mainly at weekends with my family. A park gives the children space to move and gives adults a rare chance to sit somewhere that is not surrounded by traffic or shopping.
answers.alternative_a: I visit a park several times a week because there is one beside my campus. I use it for walking, meeting friends and occasionally pretending to study.
answers.alternative_b: Quite often. I go early in the morning or after work, when the temperature is comfortable and the paths are less crowded.

questions.question: What do you usually do there?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I usually walk, do light exercise or watch my children play. Sometimes I bring a book, but in reality I spend more time looking around and making sure nobody has climbed somewhere dangerous.
answers.alternative_a: I take photos, chat with friends and buy a drink from a nearby stall. Parks are where we go when we want to meet without spending much money.
answers.alternative_b: I walk, stretch and listen to podcasts. The routine is simple, but being around trees changes the quality of the hour.

questions.question: Are there enough green spaces in your area?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: No, definitely not. My district is densely built, and the existing parks are often small or crowded. A city can add apartments quickly, but creating mature green space takes land, time and long-term planning.
answers.alternative_a: There are some attractive parks, but they are unevenly distributed. Students near the centre have options, while many residential areas have almost none.
answers.alternative_b: Da Nang has better access than many cities, especially near the river and coast, but new development still needs to protect open spaces before they disappear.

questions.question: Did you play in parks as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, constantly. The local park was our football pitch, meeting point and adventure zone. The equipment was basic, but we rarely needed anything more than space and other children.
answers.alternative_a: I did, especially on weekends with my grandparents. I remember feeding fish and competing for the swings, which seemed like the most important issue in the world.
answers.alternative_b: Yes. We played games, rode bicycles and stayed until the lights came on. Those parks felt much larger in childhood memory than they do now.

questions.question: What makes a public park attractive?
questions.quick_analysis: Identify the key factor or solution, explain how it works, and illustrate it with one practical consequence.

answers.ta_refined: Shade, cleanliness and a variety of spaces matter most. People need paths, seats, play areas and open lawns, but none of that works if the park feels unsafe or unbearably hot.
answers.alternative_a: A good park should have trees, comfortable seating and activities for different ages. Small cafes or food stalls can add life without turning it into a commercial centre.
answers.alternative_b: Accessibility is crucial. Safe paths, lighting, toilets and connections to surrounding streets determine whether a park is used daily or admired from a distance.

questions.question: Do you like flowers?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, although I appreciate them more as part of a garden than as formal bouquets. Fresh flowers add colour and life to a room, but I feel slightly guilty watching an expensive arrangement fade after a few days.
answers.alternative_a: I love flowers, especially small, natural-looking arrangements. They make ordinary spaces feel cared for and photograph beautifully.
answers.alternative_b: I like them in nature but rarely buy them. A flowering tree or field has more impact on me than flowers wrapped in plastic.

questions.question: Do you ever buy flowers for other people?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Occasionally, for birthdays, anniversaries or when someone needs encouragement. I try to choose flowers that suit the person rather than automatically buying the largest red bouquet in the shop.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, quite often for my mother and close friends. A small bunch feels warm and personal without creating pressure to find a complicated gift.
answers.alternative_b: Rarely. I usually give food or something practical, although flowers are appropriate when the gesture matters more than usefulness.

questions.question: What flowers are common in your country?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Lotus flowers are culturally important, and roses, chrysanthemums and orchids are also common. Around Tet, yellow apricot blossoms in the south and peach blossoms in the north become part of the seasonal landscape.
answers.alternative_a: Roses and sunflowers are very popular for gifts, while chrysanthemums are common in homes and at traditional occasions.
answers.alternative_b: Orchids are widely admired, especially as decorative plants. Bougainvillea and lotus flowers are also familiar across different regions.

questions.question: Have you ever grown flowers?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, with mixed success. I have grown a few flowering plants on the rooftop, but they require more attention than green plants. I learned that admiration and gardening ability are not automatically connected.
answers.alternative_a: I have grown marigolds and small roses with my mother. Some survived beautifully, and others became useful lessons in overwatering.
answers.alternative_b: Only a hardy bougainvillea plant. It tolerated heat and occasional neglect, which made it an ideal match for my gardening style.

questions.question: On what occasions do people give flowers?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: People commonly give flowers on birthdays, graduations, weddings, anniversaries and Vietnamese Women's Day. They are also used to apologise or express sympathy, so the same object can carry very different emotions depending on context.
