answers.alternative_a: Flowers are popular for romantic occasions and major achievements. Even a small bouquet can make a celebration feel more ceremonial.
answers.alternative_b: They are given at weddings, funerals, openings and family celebrations. Colour and type matter because the meaning changes with the occasion.

questions.question: Do you keep plants at home?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I keep several plants on the rooftop and near the windows. They soften the house and give me a reason to step away from screens, although some of them have survived more through resilience than expert care.
answers.alternative_a: My room has a few small plants, including a pothos and a succulent. They make the space feel calmer without demanding a full gardening routine.
answers.alternative_b: We have herbs, orchids and several large pots around the house. My parents do most of the serious care, while I provide occasional labour and enthusiastic advice.

questions.question: Who taught you how to care for plants?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: My mother taught me the basics, particularly not to water everything on the same schedule. More recently, I have learned through trial, online videos and the unfortunate evidence of plants I did not understand quickly enough.
answers.alternative_a: I learned from my grandmother, who could tell what a plant needed by touching the soil. I still rely more on reminders than instinct.
answers.alternative_b: My father taught me practical care such as pruning and repotting. He treats gardening as quiet problem-solving, which I find appealing.

questions.question: What kinds of plants are easy to grow?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: Pothos, snake plants and succulents are forgiving because they tolerate imperfect light and occasional neglect. They are ideal for beginners who want greenery without turning plant care into a second job.
answers.alternative_a: Herbs like mint and basil grow quickly if they get enough sun and water. The visible progress is encouraging for someone new to gardening.
answers.alternative_b: Snake plants and aloe vera are easy in a hot climate. They do not need daily attention and recover well from small mistakes.

questions.question: Did you help with gardening as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, though mostly under instruction. I watered vegetables, removed weeds and carried tools for older relatives. At the time it felt like work; now I understand why they found it relaxing.
answers.alternative_a: I helped my grandmother grow herbs and flowers in pots. My main contribution was watering, sometimes far more generously than the plants needed.
answers.alternative_b: A little. We had fruit trees, and I helped clear leaves and pick fruit. The reward made the work much easier to accept.

questions.question: Would you like a larger garden in the future?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: Definitely. I would love a larger garden with fruit trees, herbs and enough space for my children to move around. The dream is attractive, although the maintenance would probably be much less peaceful than the picture in my head.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially a balcony garden with flowers and herbs. I do not need a huge lawn; I just want a small green place to sit and grow things.
answers.alternative_b: I would like a practical garden with shade, vegetables and a few trees. I prefer something useful and manageable to a large decorative space that consumes every weekend.

questions.question: Do you like animals?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I do. I am especially fond of dogs because they are expressive, loyal and often seem to understand the emotional temperature of a home. I do not currently keep one, though, because affection is not a substitute for time and proper care.
answers.alternative_a: Absolutely. I love both cats and dogs, but cats probably suit my lifestyle better because they are affectionate without needing constant attention.
answers.alternative_b: I like animals, particularly dogs and birds. I enjoy observing them, although I am realistic about the responsibility involved in keeping one.

questions.question: Have you ever had a pet?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: I had a small dog when I was a teenager. He followed me everywhere and somehow knew exactly when food was being prepared. Losing him was painful, but the experience taught me why people become so attached to pets.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, my family has a cat called Mochi. She behaves as if the entire apartment belongs to her and we are merely responsible for cleaning it.
answers.alternative_b: We kept several fish and a dog when I was younger. The dog created much stronger memories, although the fish demanded far fewer emergency walks.

questions.question: What pet is popular in your country?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Dogs are probably the most popular, followed closely by cats. In cities, smaller breeds are common because apartments and busy schedules make large animals harder to manage.
answers.alternative_a: Cats have become extremely popular among young people, especially those living in apartments. Social media may have helped because cats are naturally talented content creators.
answers.alternative_b: Dogs remain the most common, although birds and ornamental fish are also popular, particularly in family homes with limited space.

questions.question: Do you think children should grow up with animals?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, provided adults take responsibility for the animal's welfare. Caring for a pet can teach empathy, patience and routine, but the lesson is lost if the child treats the animal as a temporary toy.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. Animals can help children become gentler and more confident, especially when they learn to feed, clean and respect the pet consistently.
answers.alternative_b: It can be valuable, but the choice depends on space, allergies and family time. A pet should improve the household without becoming neglected once the novelty disappears.

questions.question: What animal would you like to own if it were practical?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: If it were genuinely practical, I would have a golden retriever. They are friendly, intelligent and wonderful with families. The impractical part is that a large energetic dog needs more space and daily exercise than my current routine comfortably allows.
answers.alternative_a: I would own a rescue cat. It would fit apartment life, and giving an abandoned animal a safe home would make the choice feel meaningful.
answers.alternative_b: I would like a well-trained border collie, although its intelligence and energy would probably expose how ordinary my own daily discipline is.

questions.question: Are there many wild animals in your country?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, Vietnam has considerable wildlife diversity, from primates and elephants to marine species. The difficulty is that many animals live in protected or remote areas, so ordinary people may know they exist without ever seeing them in the wild.
answers.alternative_a: There are many species, especially in forests and national parks, although urban residents rarely encounter them. Vietnam's long coastline also supports rich marine life.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, but habitats are under pressure. The country has remarkable biodiversity, yet development and illegal trade have made some species increasingly difficult to protect.

questions.question: Have you ever seen a wild animal up close?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: The closest encounter I remember was seeing monkeys near a temple area while travelling. They looked entertaining from a distance, but once one tried to grab a bag, the experience became much more educational.
answers.alternative_a: I saw a large sea turtle while snorkelling. It moved with such calmness that everyone nearby became quiet, which was unusual for a tourist group.
answers.alternative_b: I once saw a wild deer at the edge of a forest road. The encounter lasted only seconds, but the surprise made it more memorable than many zoo visits.

questions.question: Do you enjoy wildlife documentaries?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, especially well-made documentaries that connect animal behaviour with habitat and conservation. They can make a distant ecosystem feel intimate without pretending that nature is always gentle or tidy.
answers.alternative_a: I love them. High-quality filming shows details people could never observe safely, and the storytelling often turns one animal's survival into a complete drama.
answers.alternative_b: I watch them occasionally, mainly programmes about oceans and predators. I prefer documentaries that explain the science rather than giving animals overly human personalities.

questions.question: Which wild animal would you most like to see?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: I would most like to see elephants in the wild. Their size is impressive, but what fascinates me more is their social behaviour and memory. I would want the encounter to be ethical and distant, not arranged for a photograph.
answers.alternative_a: I would love to see a whale. The idea of an animal that enormous moving quietly through the ocean is difficult to imagine from a screen.
answers.alternative_b: A snow leopard would be extraordinary because it is so elusive. Realistically, seeing one would require more patience, cold and mountain travel than I currently possess.

questions.question: Should wild animals be kept in zoos?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Zoos should exist only when conservation, research and animal welfare are genuine priorities. Keeping a species in a cramped enclosure for entertainment is difficult to defend, but responsible breeding and rescue programmes can still play an important role.
answers.alternative_a: Some should, particularly endangered animals that cannot safely return to the wild. However, the living conditions need to reflect natural behaviour rather than visitor convenience.
answers.alternative_b: I prefer wildlife sanctuaries, but well-managed zoos can educate the public and fund conservation. The key question is whether the institution serves the animals or simply displays them.

questions.question: What is the weather usually like where you live?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: Ho Chi Minh City is hot and humid for most of the year, with a dry season and a rainy season rather than four clear seasons. The heat is manageable indoors, but stepping outside at midday can feel like opening an oven door.
answers.alternative_a: Hanoi has hot summers, cool winters and fairly distinct seasonal changes. The transitions are pleasant, although humidity makes both heat and cold feel stronger.
answers.alternative_b: Da Nang is generally warm and coastal, with a sunny dry season and heavy rain later in the year. Sea breezes help, but storms can be intense.

questions.question: What kind of weather do you enjoy most?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: I enjoy cool, dry weather with light sunshine. It is comfortable enough for walking, working and sleeping without needing constant air conditioning, so ordinary life simply becomes easier.
answers.alternative_a: I love crisp autumn weather. The air feels lighter, clothes are more comfortable and the city seems calmer after the summer heat.
answers.alternative_b: Warm, breezy weather is ideal for me. I want enough sun for the beach, but not the kind of heat that makes every movement feel unnecessary.

questions.question: Does weather affect your mood?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Definitely. Long periods of heat make me impatient and less willing to go outside, whereas a cool morning can improve my mood before anything else happens. I wish I were less affected, but the pattern is obvious.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, grey rainy days make me slower, while bright cool weather gives me energy. It is not dramatic, but it influences how social and productive I feel.
answers.alternative_b: A little. Stormy weather makes me cautious and restless, but ordinary changes do not affect me as much as lack of sleep or work pressure.

questions.question: What do you do on very hot days?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I stay indoors during the hottest hours, drink plenty of water and move exercise to early morning or evening. If I must go out, I plan the route carefully because direct sun can turn a short errand into a test of character.
answers.alternative_a: I visit air-conditioned places, wear light clothing and carry water everywhere. Ice tea also becomes less a drink and more a survival strategy.
answers.alternative_b: I swim or go to the coast early, then avoid outdoor activity at midday. In the evening, I open the windows if the sea breeze is strong enough.

questions.question: Has the weather in your hometown changed?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, it feels more unpredictable. Hot periods seem longer, and heavy rain can arrive suddenly with greater intensity. I cannot prove every memory with data, but local people frequently make the same observation.
answers.alternative_a: The summers feel hotter and extreme rain seems more common. Seasonal boundaries are also less reliable than when I was a child.
answers.alternative_b: There appear to be more unusually hot days and stronger storms. Coastal development may also make flooding and heat feel more noticeable.

questions.question: What is your favorite season?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: The closest thing to a favourite season for me is the cooler part of the dry season, around the end of the year. The air is less oppressive, evenings are pleasant and simply walking outside stops feeling like a punishment.
answers.alternative_a: Autumn is my favourite. Hanoi becomes cooler and drier, the light is beautiful and the streets smell of milk flowers, which is lovely unless the scent becomes overwhelming.
answers.alternative_b: I prefer summer because the sea is at its best and outdoor plans are easier. I accept the heat in exchange for long bright days.

questions.question: What do people usually do during that season?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: People spend more time outdoors, travel and prepare for year-end celebrations. In the south, the pleasant weather also makes weddings and family gatherings much easier to organise.
answers.alternative_a: During autumn, people walk around lakes, take photographs and enjoy seasonal food. The city becomes more comfortable, so even ordinary evenings feel more social.
answers.alternative_b: Summer is when people go to the beach, travel with family and organise outdoor events. Coastal businesses become much busier as well.

questions.question: Are the seasons clearly different where you live?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not clearly. In southern Vietnam, the main distinction is between wet and dry periods, and the temperature remains fairly high. Seasonal change is something I notice more through rainfall and festivals than leaves or snow.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, Hanoi has recognisable spring, summer, autumn and winter, although the length and intensity vary. That variety is one of the city's charms.
answers.alternative_b: There are mainly dry and rainy seasons. Temperatures shift, but the coastal climate does not create four sharply different landscapes.

questions.question: Did you prefer a different season as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I loved summer holidays because they meant freedom from school, trips to my hometown and entire afternoons outdoors. As an adult, summer mostly means higher electricity bills and searching for shade.
answers.alternative_a: As a child, winter was my favourite because new coats and hot food felt exciting. Now I prefer autumn because it is comfortable without being harsh.
answers.alternative_b: I preferred the rainy season as a child because storms meant indoor games and occasional school closures. Adult responsibilities have made that weather less charming.

questions.question: Would you like to experience a snowy winter?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: I would, at least once. A real snowy winter looks beautiful and completely different from anything I grew up with. I would enjoy the first few days enormously and probably begin complaining about frozen fingers soon afterwards.
answers.alternative_a: Absolutely. I want to see fresh snow, build a snowman and experience a proper winter market, although I would need advice on clothing.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, for a short trip. Snow is visually appealing, but months of ice, heating costs and dark afternoons would be a much harder lifestyle test.

questions.question: Do you like rainy weather?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I like gentle rain when I am safely indoors or have nowhere urgent to go. The sound is calming and the temperature drops, but heavy rain during a commute removes every poetic quality very quickly.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially light rain in the evening. It makes the city quieter and gives me an excellent excuse to stay home with tea and a film.
answers.alternative_b: Only in moderation. Rain is welcome after hot days, but prolonged wet weather affects travel and makes everything feel damp.

questions.question: What do you usually do when it rains?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: If I am at home, I read, work or listen to music near a window. If I am outside, the routine is less romantic: find shelter, protect my laptop and hope the road is not already flooded.
answers.alternative_a: I usually study in a cafe or stay home and cook something warm. Rain makes indoor activities feel more deliberate rather than boring.
answers.alternative_b: I postpone non-essential trips and work on indoor projects. If the rain is light, I still go for a short drive because the coast looks dramatic.

questions.question: Does heavy rain cause problems where you live?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, serious problems. Some streets flood quickly, traffic slows to a crawl and motorbikes are particularly vulnerable. A thirty-minute journey can double, so heavy rain affects both safety and schedules.
answers.alternative_a: It can cause flooding and public transport delays. The inconvenience is worst during rush hour when drainage systems are already under pressure.
answers.alternative_b: Heavy rain and storms can flood lower areas and disrupt coastal travel. The city has improved drainage, but extreme weather still exposes weaknesses.

questions.question: Did you enjoy playing in the rain as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Absolutely. My friends and I splashed through puddles and treated getting soaked as part of the fun. Adults saw wet clothes and mud; we saw a temporary playground.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, although my mother never shared my enthusiasm. I loved paper boats and running outside during warm summer rain.
answers.alternative_b: I did, especially during short tropical showers. The enjoyment ended only when we had to clean the floor and explain the state of our clothes.

questions.question: Do you check the weather forecast before going out?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, particularly during the rainy season. A quick forecast helps me decide whether to carry a raincoat, leave earlier or move an outdoor plan. I still get surprised, but at least it is an informed surprise.
answers.alternative_a: I check it every morning because my travel depends on buses and walking. The hourly forecast is more useful than the general daily symbol.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, mainly for wind and storm warnings. Coastal weather can change quickly, so checking conditions is a practical habit rather than an obsession.

questions.question: Do you often look at the sky?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, especially from the rooftop in the early morning or at sunset. Looking up is a small way to interrupt a day spent staring at documents and screens, and the city feels less confined for a moment.
answers.alternative_a: Quite often. I photograph clouds, sunsets and changing light, so the sky is one of the few subjects that is always available but never exactly repeated.
answers.alternative_b: I do, mainly near the coast where the horizon is open. Weather and light are easier to understand when I actually pay attention to the sky.

questions.question: What time of day is the sky most beautiful?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Sunset is the most beautiful for me. The colours change quickly, buildings become silhouettes and even an ordinary city view can look cinematic for ten minutes.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer early morning, when the light is soft and the sky feels clean before traffic and heat build up.
answers.alternative_b: Just after sunset is my favourite. The remaining blue light and the first city lights create a calm transition rather than a dramatic display.

questions.question: Can you see many stars where you live?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not many. Light pollution and tall buildings hide most stars, so on a clear night I may see a few bright ones. The difference becomes striking whenever I travel to the countryside.
answers.alternative_a: Very few in central Hanoi. I usually need to leave the city before the sky becomes properly dark.
answers.alternative_b: More than in larger cities, especially along quieter beaches, but the view is still nothing compared with remote mountain areas.

questions.question: Did you learn about the stars at school?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, the basics: planets, the solar system and a few constellations. I found the scale fascinating, but the lessons were brief, so most of my detailed knowledge later came from documentaries.
answers.alternative_a: We did a short unit in science class and once used a simple telescope. Seeing the moon's surface made the topic feel real for the first time.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, particularly the physics of stars and planets. I enjoyed it, although the enormous distances were difficult to grasp intuitively.

questions.question: Would you like to learn more about astronomy?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: I would. Astronomy places everyday worries in an interesting perspective, and I would love to understand what I am actually seeing rather than calling every bright point a star.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. I want to learn the main constellations and try astrophotography, even if my first images are just blurred dots.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, especially the technology behind telescopes and space missions. The combination of engineering and fundamental questions is hard to resist.

questions.question: What kind of food do you enjoy most?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: I enjoy Vietnamese food most, particularly dishes with fresh herbs, balanced flavours and broth. I can appreciate international cuisine, but a well-made bowl of noodles still feels comforting in a way that more elaborate food often does not.
answers.alternative_a: I love spicy Asian food, especially Korean and Thai dishes. Strong flavours make a meal exciting, although I sometimes overestimate how much heat I can handle.
answers.alternative_b: Seafood is my favourite, particularly grilled fish and shellfish. Growing up near the coast made freshness more important to me than complicated presentation.

questions.question: Do you prefer home-cooked food or restaurant food?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Home-cooked food most of the time. It is healthier, more affordable and connected to family routines. Restaurant meals are enjoyable precisely because they are occasional and free everyone from cooking and washing up.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer restaurant food for variety, especially when meeting friends. At home I eat simply, so eating out is where I try dishes I cannot prepare myself.
answers.alternative_b: Home cooking, provided someone has time. I like controlling ingredients and portion sizes, but restaurants are useful when convenience matters more than perfection.

questions.question: Is there any food you dislike?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I dislike food with an extremely strong fermented smell. I know some dishes are culturally valued and may taste better than they smell, but my nose often makes the decision before my curiosity can intervene.
answers.alternative_a: I am not keen on overly fatty meat. The texture puts me off, even when the seasoning is excellent.
answers.alternative_b: Very sweet savoury dishes do not appeal to me. I prefer clear flavours and find heavy sauces tiring after a few bites.

questions.question: Have your eating habits changed?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I eat more deliberately now. I include more vegetables, reduce sugary drinks and pay attention to portion size. I am not perfectly disciplined, but health has moved from an abstract idea to something I can feel in daily energy.
answers.alternative_a: I cook more and order less than I did in my first university year. Budget is one reason, but I also feel better when meals are less oily.
answers.alternative_b: My diet has become higher in protein and more regular since I started training seriously. I also drink less alcohol because recovery makes the effect impossible to ignore.

questions.question: What dish would you recommend to a visitor?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I would recommend pho or banh xeo, depending on what the visitor likes. Pho is comforting and widely available, while a crisp banh xeo with herbs and dipping sauce gives a more interactive, distinctly Vietnamese experience.
answers.alternative_a: Bun cha would be my choice. Grilled pork, noodles, herbs and dipping sauce are easy to enjoy, and the meal feels informal and social.
answers.alternative_b: I would recommend mi Quang from central Vietnam. The noodles, herbs, peanuts and small amount of rich broth create a flavour that is difficult to confuse with any other dish.

questions.question: Do you enjoy cooking?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I enjoy cooking when I have time and a clear recipe. It can be relaxing and creative, but on a busy weekday the same activity becomes a race involving several pans and one hungry family.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially simple dishes I can share with friends. Cooking gives me a sense of achievement because the result is immediate and usually edible.
answers.alternative_b: I like practical cooking rather than elaborate presentation. Preparing a good meal efficiently is satisfying, although I do not dream about spending an entire afternoon decorating one plate.

questions.question: How often do you cook?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: A few times a week, mainly breakfast or dinner. My wife and I share the responsibility, so I am not the household chef, but I can handle enough dishes to prevent starvation and boredom.
answers.alternative_a: I cook almost every day because eating out is expensive. Weekday meals are simple, while weekends are when I try something new.
answers.alternative_b: Three or four times a week. I prepare meals in batches so that workdays do not end with another major decision.

questions.question: Who taught you to cook?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: My mother taught me the basics, such as balancing seasoning and knowing when food is actually cooked rather than merely brown. Later, videos and repeated mistakes expanded the menu.
answers.alternative_a: I learned from my grandmother and online recipes. She taught intuition; the Internet supplies exact measurements when my intuition is unreliable.
answers.alternative_b: My father taught me grilled and seafood dishes. For everything else, I rely on recipes and the useful ability to taste as I go.

questions.question: What dish can you make well?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I make a reliable cheese omelette and a decent spaghetti carbonara. Neither is complex, but I have learned the timing well enough that the eggs stay soft and the pasta does not become a heavy cream sauce.
answers.alternative_a: I can make Vietnamese spring rolls quite well. The preparation takes time, but arranging the ingredients and rolling them together is almost therapeutic.
answers.alternative_b: Grilled fish is my best dish. I keep the seasoning simple and focus on freshness, temperature and not destroying it through overcooking.

questions.question: Would you like to improve your cooking skills?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: Definitely. I would like to become confident with a wider range of healthy family meals, especially dishes that can be prepared quickly. The real goal is not restaurant-level skill; it is variety without spending the whole evening in the kitchen.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, I want to improve baking. It demands more precision than my usual cooking, and I like the idea of making bread or cakes from scratch.
answers.alternative_b: I would like to learn more vegetarian cooking. It would broaden my diet and teach me to build flavour without relying on meat as the centre of every meal.

questions.question: How often do you eat at restaurants?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: Probably once or twice a week, usually with my family or when meeting friends. Eating out is convenient and social, but doing it every day would be expensive and would make restaurant meals feel less special.
answers.alternative_a: Two or three times a week. My university schedule is irregular, so cafes and inexpensive restaurants often fill the gap between classes.
answers.alternative_b: About once a week. I prefer home meals on workdays and use restaurants for weekends, celebrations or trying a cuisine we cannot cook well.

questions.question: What kind of restaurant do you prefer?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: I prefer relaxed, mid-priced restaurants with a focused menu and enough space to talk. I care more about food, cleanliness and service than elaborate decoration or a waiter describing every ingredient like a poem.
answers.alternative_a: I like small modern restaurants that serve Asian fusion food. A lively atmosphere and creative menu make the evening feel like an experience rather than just a meal.
answers.alternative_b: Seafood restaurants near the coast are my favourite. Fresh ingredients, simple cooking and an open view matter more to me than formal service.

questions.question: What makes a restaurant worth returning to?
questions.quick_analysis: Identify the key factor or solution, explain how it works, and illustrate it with one practical consequence.

answers.ta_refined: Consistency is the key. A restaurant earns my return when the food tastes good on different visits, staff handle problems politely and the final bill feels fair. One brilliant dish cannot rescue unreliable service forever.
answers.alternative_a: I return when a place has one or two dishes I genuinely crave and an atmosphere where I can relax. Friendly staff who remember regular customers make a huge difference.
answers.alternative_b: Quality and honesty matter most. I want fresh food, clear prices and portions that match the description. Reliable basics create more loyalty than fashionable interiors.

questions.question: Do you usually try new dishes when eating out?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Sometimes, but not recklessly. I usually order one familiar dish and one new item to share. That way curiosity does not leave the entire table hungry if the experiment goes wrong.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, almost always. Trying something new is one of the main reasons I eat out, and friends make the risk easier because we can share.
answers.alternative_b: Only when the menu explains the dish clearly or the staff recommend it. I enjoy variety, but I do not like paying to discover that an ingredient I dislike is central.

questions.question: Have restaurant habits changed in your city?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, eating out has become more frequent and more varied. Delivery apps, international chains and social media trends have expanded choices, but they have also made restaurants compete on appearance as much as taste.
answers.alternative_a: People now treat cafes and restaurants as places to work, photograph and socialise, not merely eat. New concepts appear quickly and disappear just as fast.
answers.alternative_b: There are far more delivery-focused businesses and specialised restaurants. Customers expect online reviews, digital menus and fast service, which has changed how even traditional places operate.

questions.question: Do you usually eat breakfast?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, almost every day. I am not pleasant or productive on an empty stomach, so breakfast is less a health slogan and more a practical form of damage control.
answers.alternative_a: Usually, although I sometimes skip it when I have an early class. I notice the difference by mid-morning because concentration becomes much harder.
answers.alternative_b: Yes. I prefer a simple breakfast to starting work hungry, especially on days when lunch may be delayed.

questions.question: What do you normally have in the morning?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I usually have eggs, bread and coffee, or a bowl of noodles if I have more time. The meal is fairly repetitive, but mornings are not when I want a long decision-making process.
answers.alternative_a: I have yoghurt, fruit and sometimes a banh mi on the way to university. It depends on whether I leave home calmly or at the last possible minute.
answers.alternative_b: I normally eat oats, eggs or leftover rice with something simple. I focus on protein and convenience rather than creating a photogenic breakfast.

questions.question: Is breakfast important to you?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Very important. It gives me energy for teaching and prevents me becoming distracted by hunger during the first class. A good breakfast does not solve the day, but skipping it creates an unnecessary problem.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, because my mornings are long. Without breakfast, I end up buying sugary snacks and spending more money later.
answers.alternative_b: It matters on working days, especially if I train in the morning. I do not believe everyone needs the same routine, but my body performs better with one.

questions.question: Was your breakfast different when you were a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Quite different. As a child, I often ate rice or noodles prepared by my mother, and breakfast was a family routine. Now it is faster, lighter and sometimes eaten while checking the day's schedule.
answers.alternative_a: I ate more traditional hot dishes as a child because my family prepared them. University life has replaced many of those breakfasts with yoghurt or food bought outside.
answers.alternative_b: Childhood breakfast was larger and less planned around nutrition. I ate what was served, whereas now I choose food based on work and exercise.

questions.question: Would you rather eat at home or buy breakfast outside?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: At home, because it is cheaper, calmer and easier to control. Buying breakfast outside is useful on rushed days, but I prefer not to begin every morning in a queue.
answers.alternative_a: I like buying breakfast outside because there are so many inexpensive choices near campus. It also creates a small social moment before class.
answers.alternative_b: At home on weekdays, outside at weekends. Home is efficient; a slow breakfast at a local shop is part of relaxing.

questions.question: Do you often eat snacks?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not very often. I try to eat proper meals, but if I have a long gap between classes, I reach for nuts, fruit or whatever is nearest. The dangerous snacks are the ones that appear beside my laptop without a conscious decision.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, probably twice a day. I usually have something small between lectures, especially when lunch is late. Snacks are also my weakness during group study sessions.
answers.alternative_b: Occasionally, mainly after exercise or during long work sessions. I prefer planned snacks because random eating can quietly become an extra meal.

questions.question: What is your favorite snack?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: Roasted cashews are my favourite because they are crunchy, filling and easy to keep at work. I have to portion them, though; eating directly from the bag turns a healthy snack into an unexpectedly large commitment.
answers.alternative_a: I love yoghurt with fruit and granola. It tastes like a treat but still feels fresh enough that I do not regret it afterwards.
answers.alternative_b: I usually choose dried squid or roasted peanuts. They are savoury, portable and go well with tea, although the smell can make them unpopular in an office.

questions.question: Did you eat different snacks as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, childhood snacks were sweeter and much less supervised. I loved colourful ice pops, instant noodles eaten dry and cheap sweets from the school gate. Nutrition was not part of the conversation.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. I ate chips, candy and small cakes after school. Now I still enjoy them, but I notice the sugar and price in a way children rarely do.
answers.alternative_b: I ate more street snacks as a child, especially grilled corn and rice crackers. They were simple, social and tied to afternoons with friends.

questions.question: Do you prefer sweet or savory snacks?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Savoury, without hesitation. I would choose nuts, crackers or popcorn over cake most days. Sweet food is enjoyable for a few bites, but savoury snacks are much harder for me to stop eating.
answers.alternative_a: I have a sweet tooth, especially for chocolate and pastries. I try to keep portions sensible, but a good bakery can defeat excellent intentions.
answers.alternative_b: Savoury snacks suit me better. I like strong flavours and find very sweet food tiring after a while.

questions.question: Are healthy snacks easy to find where you live?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: They are available, but convenience is uneven. Supermarkets sell fruit, yoghurt and nuts, while small shops often display sugary drinks and fried snacks most prominently. Healthy choices exist; they just require slightly more planning.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially around universities where shops offer fruit cups, yoghurt and low-sugar drinks. The healthier option is usually more expensive, though.
answers.alternative_b: They are fairly easy to find in larger stores, but not always in workplaces or transport areas. Preparation at home remains the cheapest solution.

questions.question: What do you usually drink during the day?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: Water and coffee are the two constants in my day. I start with coffee, then try to keep a bottle of water nearby because teaching for hours makes dehydration surprisingly easy to ignore.
answers.alternative_a: I drink water, green tea and the occasional milk tea. The last one is more of a reward than hydration, despite what I sometimes tell myself.
answers.alternative_b: Mostly water and unsweetened tea. I also have one coffee in the morning, but I avoid turning caffeine into an all-day supply system.

questions.question: Do you prefer tea or coffee?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Coffee, especially in the morning. I like tea, but coffee creates a clear starting signal for the day. The ritual matters almost as much as the caffeine.
answers.alternative_a: Tea. I enjoy the lighter taste and can drink it slowly without feeling overstimulated. Jasmine tea is my usual choice.
answers.alternative_b: I prefer coffee for concentration and tea for relaxation. If forced to choose one, coffee would win because it is part of my work routine.

questions.question: How much water do you drink?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: Roughly two litres, although the amount increases on hot or active days. I use a large bottle because visual evidence works better than vague promises to drink more.
answers.alternative_a: Probably one and a half litres. I am trying to improve because I often realise late in the day that coffee has done most of the work.
answers.alternative_b: Around two to three litres, particularly when I exercise. I track it loosely rather than measuring every glass.

questions.question: Is there a drink you avoid?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I avoid very sugary energy drinks. They give a brief lift followed by a crash, and the sweetness is often overwhelming. If I need energy, sleep would be the better answer, though coffee is the more realistic one.
answers.alternative_a: I rarely drink fizzy soft drinks because they make me feel bloated and do not actually satisfy thirst.
answers.alternative_b: I avoid sweet bottled tea. It looks healthier than soda, but some versions contain enough sugar to make the label rather misleading.

questions.question: Have your drinking habits changed over time?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I drink more water and less alcohol than I did in my twenties. The change was not a dramatic resolution; I simply became less willing to lose sleep and energy for the sake of a late night.
answers.alternative_a: I drink less milk tea now because the habit became expensive and sugary. Tea and coffee have replaced it on most days.
answers.alternative_b: My habits are more consistent. I used to drink coffee whenever tired, whereas now I limit caffeine after lunch and focus more on water.

questions.question: Do you enjoy shopping?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not really my thing. I end up at the mall with my family fairly often, but I am mostly there to keep the children entertained while my wife does the real shopping. I follow, carry bags and offer opinions only when specifically requested.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially when I am not searching for anything urgent. Browsing clothes, books and small design shops can be relaxing, although crowded sales make me lose enthusiasm quickly.
answers.alternative_b: Only when the purchase has a clear purpose. I enjoy researching products, but wandering through shops without a plan feels tiring rather than entertaining.

questions.question: What do you usually shop for?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: Mostly books, household items and technology. Clothes are bought when necessary, not as a hobby. I am far more likely to compare three keyboards than three shirts.
answers.alternative_a: I shop for clothes, skincare, stationery and gifts. I also spend too much time in bookshops even when I promised myself I was only looking.
answers.alternative_b: I usually buy electronics, sports gear and practical household supplies. My purchases are not glamorous, but they tend to be used.

questions.question: Do you prefer shopping online or in stores?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Online for routine or standardised products, in stores for clothes, furniture and anything where size or feel matters. Convenience is useful, but returning the wrong item can erase the time saved.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer stores because I enjoy trying things and discovering products I did not search for. I use online shopping when a particular item is unavailable locally.
answers.alternative_b: Online shopping suits me because I can compare specifications and prices calmly. For expensive purchases, I still visit a store before deciding.

questions.question: Who do you usually go shopping with?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: Usually with my wife and children, although our goals are not always aligned. My wife wants to browse, the children want entertainment and I want to finish efficiently, so compromise is built into the trip.
answers.alternative_a: I go with friends because we give honest opinions and turn the outing into a social activity. For serious purchases, I sometimes go alone to avoid distraction.
answers.alternative_b: Mostly alone. I know what I need, and shopping is faster without negotiating pace or stopping at every unrelated shop.

questions.question: Have your shopping habits changed recently?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I buy more online and make fewer spontaneous purchases. Reading reviews and comparing prices has become automatic, although targeted advertising occasionally finds a weakness I did not know I had.
answers.alternative_a: I shop more selectively because I am trying to reduce clutter. I still enjoy fashion, but I ask whether I will use an item repeatedly rather than whether it looks exciting for five minutes.
answers.alternative_b: My habits have become more planned. I keep a list, wait before buying non-essential items and prioritise durability over the lowest initial price.

questions.question: Are you interested in fashion?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not particularly. I want clothes to fit well, look presentable and require very little thought. I notice fashion trends, but I do not feel obliged to reorganise my wardrobe every time one appears.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, quite a lot. I enjoy following trends and adapting them to my own style rather than copying an entire look.
answers.alternative_b: Only mildly. I appreciate good design and materials, but I care more about function than seasonal fashion.

questions.question: What kinds of clothes do you usually wear?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: I usually wear polo shirts or plain shirts with trousers for work, and T-shirts with shorts at home. The colours are mostly neutral, which makes getting dressed quick and reduces the chance of an ambitious mismatch.
answers.alternative_a: My style is casual and feminine: loose trousers, simple tops, dresses and light jackets. I like pieces that can work for both class and meeting friends.
answers.alternative_b: I wear T-shirts, jeans or technical trousers, plus trainers. At work the dress code is relaxed, so comfort and clean lines matter most.

questions.question: Do you choose comfort or style?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Comfort first, but not comfort alone. Clothes should allow me to move and concentrate, yet I still want to look appropriate for the setting. The ideal outfit is one I forget about after putting it on.
answers.alternative_a: I try to balance both. A stylish item that is painful will stay in the wardrobe, while purely comfortable clothes can make me feel underdressed.
answers.alternative_b: Comfort wins. I prefer simple clothes that fit properly and survive regular use; style is welcome if it does not create extra maintenance.

questions.question: Did you care more about fashion when you were younger?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Probably. In my twenties, I cared more about brands and whether an outfit looked impressive. Now I pay greater attention to quality and fit, which may be less exciting but saves money and embarrassment.
answers.alternative_a: I care more now because fashion has become a creative interest. As a teenager, I was self-conscious and mostly copied what friends wore.
answers.alternative_b: I cared slightly more as a student because clothes helped signal identity. Work and exercise have made practicality more important.

questions.question: Is there an item of clothing you wear frequently?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I wear a lightweight navy jacket constantly. It works in air-conditioned rooms, light rain and slightly formal situations, so it has become the item I grab without thinking.
answers.alternative_a: A pair of wide-leg black trousers appears in my wardrobe several times a week. They are comfortable, easy to style and somehow make a simple top look deliberate.
answers.alternative_b: I frequently wear a grey sports watch. It tracks exercise, handles notifications and is durable enough that I never need to think about it.

questions.question: How many pairs of shoes do you own?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: Around eight pairs, which is probably fewer than average but enough for every real situation. I have work shoes, trainers, sandals and a couple of pairs that survive mainly because throwing them away feels wasteful.
answers.alternative_a: Probably fifteen pairs. Some are practical, while others exist because they looked excellent in the shop and turned out to be less cooperative in real life.
answers.alternative_b: About six pairs. I prefer using shoes until they are genuinely worn out rather than collecting alternatives.

questions.question: What kind of shoes do you wear most?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: Trainers, by a large margin. They are comfortable for teaching, walking and family outings, and modern designs look presentable enough for most casual situations.
answers.alternative_a: I wear white trainers most often because they match almost everything. Keeping them white is the part the fashion photographs do not explain.
answers.alternative_b: Running shoes are my default. They support long days on my feet and can move from commuting to light exercise without a change.

questions.question: Do you buy shoes online?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Rarely. Size may be standard, but width, cushioning and shape vary too much. I prefer trying shoes on because an easy return policy does not prevent an uncomfortable first week.
answers.alternative_a: Sometimes, but only from brands whose sizing I know. For a new style, I visit a shop because photographs hide how a shoe actually feels.
answers.alternative_b: I research online but usually buy in person. Fit is technical, and a few millimetres can determine whether the purchase is excellent or useless.

questions.question: Did you have a favorite pair as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, a pair of light-up trainers. Every step made the soles flash, and I considered them the height of technology. I wore them until the lights failed and the shoes were visibly too small.
answers.alternative_a: I loved red canvas shoes in primary school. They were inexpensive, but I felt unusually confident whenever I wore them.
answers.alternative_b: My favourite pair was a set of football boots. They did not improve my ability nearly as much as I expected, but I treated them like professional equipment.

questions.question: What matters most when choosing shoes?
questions.quick_analysis: Identify the key factor or solution, explain how it works, and illustrate it with one practical consequence.

answers.ta_refined: Comfort and fit come first, followed by durability. A beautiful shoe that creates pain after twenty minutes is not fashionable; it is simply an expensive problem.
answers.alternative_a: Comfort matters most, but design is a close second. I want shoes that support a full day and still make the outfit feel finished.
answers.alternative_b: Fit, grip and construction are essential. I choose based on how and where the shoes will be used, not just appearance.

questions.question: Do you carry a bag every day?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I carry a backpack on most working days. It holds a laptop, chargers and teaching materials, so calling it an accessory is slightly generous; it is closer to a mobile office.
answers.alternative_a: I carry a tote or small shoulder bag every day. Going out without one feels strange because my phone alone cannot hold the collection of things I might need.
answers.alternative_b: I use a compact backpack for work and a small waist bag for short trips. I prefer keeping my hands free.

questions.question: What do you usually keep in it?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: A laptop, charger, notebook, pens, water bottle and several small items that seemed essential when packed. There is usually also one cable whose purpose I cannot immediately explain.
answers.alternative_a: I keep my wallet, phone, cosmetics, earphones, tissues and a small notebook. The contents are ordinary, but finding one item quickly is still a challenge.
answers.alternative_b: I carry a laptop, battery pack, water bottle, keys and basic first-aid items. Everything has a fixed place because searching annoys me.

questions.question: Do you prefer practical or fashionable accessories?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Practical, without question. I want something light, durable and organised, although good design is welcome. An accessory that looks beautiful but cannot survive rain or hold what I need has misunderstood its job.
answers.alternative_a: I like a balance. A bag should be useful, but accessories are also an easy way to make simple clothes more personal.
answers.alternative_b: Practical. I prefer neutral colours, strong zips and enough compartments. Fashion changes; a broken strap changes the whole day.

questions.question: Have you ever lost a bag?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I once left a backpack in a taxi. I realised within minutes and managed to contact the driver, but the brief period when my laptop, documents and calmness had disappeared was extremely unpleasant.
answers.alternative_a: I lost a small handbag at a festival and never recovered it. Fortunately, it contained little money, but replacing cards and keys was a painful lesson.
answers.alternative_b: I misplaced a bag at an airport cafe. Security found it, and the experience permanently improved my habit of checking the chair before leaving.

questions.question: Would you spend a lot of money on an accessory?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: Only for exceptional quality and long-term use. I would pay more for a work bag that protects expensive equipment and lasts for years, but not simply for a visible logo.
answers.alternative_a: Possibly, if the design were timeless and I knew I would use it constantly. I would still set a limit because accessories are easy to romanticise.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, for specialised items such as a durable watch or travel backpack. Performance and reliability can justify cost; status cannot.

questions.question: Do you enjoy giving gifts?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, especially when I know the person well enough to choose something that fits their life. The best part is not the object itself but the moment they realise I remembered a small detail.
answers.alternative_a: I love giving gifts. Planning and wrapping them is enjoyable, although I sometimes create unnecessary pressure by wanting every present to feel original.
answers.alternative_b: I do, but I prefer simple, useful gifts. I would rather give one thoughtful item than an impressive object that becomes clutter.

questions.question: What kinds of gifts do you like receiving?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: I like receiving books, food or something connected to a hobby. These gifts show attention without requiring the giver to guess my size, style or willingness to display a decorative object forever.
answers.alternative_a: I enjoy personalised gifts, such as a photo book or handmade item. The effort often matters more than the price.
answers.alternative_b: Practical items are ideal: quality tools, sports gear or technology I will actually use. I appreciate sentiment, but usefulness keeps the gift present in daily life.

questions.question: When did you last give someone a present?
questions.quick_analysis: Anchor the answer in a clear time, add one vivid detail, and connect the memory to how you see it now.

answers.ta_refined: I recently gave my wife a small photo album for our anniversary. It took longer to choose the pictures than to buy a conventional gift, but the shared memories made it feel far more personal.
answers.alternative_a: Last week, I bought a friend a set of art markers for her birthday. She had mentioned them months earlier, so the surprise came from being remembered.
answers.alternative_b: I gave my father a new set of gardening tools. It was not dramatic, but he used them the same afternoon, which felt like strong approval.

questions.question: Do you prefer useful or surprising gifts?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Useful with a small element of surprise. A practical gift can still feel special if it reflects the person's interests or solves a problem they casually mentioned.
answers.alternative_a: Surprising gifts are more exciting, provided the giver understands the recipient. A surprise that ignores taste becomes a social test.
answers.alternative_b: Useful gifts. Novelty fades quickly, while something well chosen can improve a routine for years.

questions.question: Is choosing a gift difficult for you?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: It can be difficult because I want the gift to feel personal without creating waste. I listen for clues throughout the year, which is more reliable than trying to become inspired two days before a birthday.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially for people who seem to own everything. I often choose an experience or consumable item so the gift does not add clutter.
answers.alternative_b: Moderately. I make a list of the person's interests, budget and actual needs, which turns an emotional puzzle into a manageable decision.

questions.question: Do you usually carry cash?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Only a small amount. Digital payments are accepted almost everywhere I go, but I keep some cash for markets, parking or the moment technology decides not to cooperate.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, although less than before. Small food stalls and transport sometimes still require cash, so I do not feel comfortable carrying none.
answers.alternative_b: Very little. I pay by card or phone whenever possible because it creates a record and reduces the need for change.

questions.question: What do you spend most of your money on?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: Housing, family expenses and education take the largest share. Books and technology also appear regularly, usually under the optimistic label of professional investment.
answers.alternative_a: Most of my money goes on rent, food and transport. After that, I spend on clothes, cafes and occasional trips with friends.
answers.alternative_b: Living costs and savings come first, followed by fitness and technology. I try to spend more on things that improve daily life than on short-lived entertainment.

questions.question: Did you receive pocket money as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, a small weekly amount. My parents expected me to divide it between snacks and savings, although the snacks usually presented a stronger argument.
answers.alternative_a: I received pocket money from secondary school onwards. It taught me basic choices because spending everything on Monday made the rest of the week painfully educational.
answers.alternative_b: Only occasionally. I earned small amounts by helping with family work, which made me more careful because the money was connected to effort.

questions.question: Is it easy for you to manage money?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Generally yes, because I track major expenses and save automatically. I still make imperfect choices, but a system prevents one impulsive purchase from quietly becoming a habit.
answers.alternative_a: I am learning. I can manage a monthly budget, but irregular costs such as travel or repairs still catch me by surprise.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, fairly easy. I separate essential spending, savings and discretionary money, which reduces the number of decisions I have to make.

questions.question: Do you think money can buy happiness?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: It can buy comfort, security and opportunities, all of which contribute to happiness. What it cannot buy is meaning or a healthy relationship, so money is powerful but incomplete rather than irrelevant.
answers.alternative_a: Up to a point. Having enough removes stress and creates choices, but constantly comparing wealth can make even a comfortable person dissatisfied.
answers.alternative_b: Money can support happiness by protecting time and health. Beyond basic freedom, however, the return becomes less predictable because habits and relationships matter more.

questions.question: Do you try to save money?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I save automatically at the beginning of each month rather than waiting to see what remains. If saving is the final step, daily expenses have a remarkable ability to consume the entire plan.
answers.alternative_a: I try to, although the amount changes. I use a separate account so the money feels less available for casual spending.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, consistently. I treat savings as a fixed expense and divide it between emergencies, investment and specific goals.

questions.question: What are you currently saving for?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I am saving for a major home renovation and a larger education project. Both goals are expensive, so progress is gradual, but seeing the amount grow makes the future plan feel concrete.
answers.alternative_a: I am saving for a graduation trip to Japan. Having a clear destination makes it easier to skip small purchases that would otherwise feel harmless.
answers.alternative_b: I am building an emergency fund and saving towards an electric car. The emergency fund is less exciting, but it deserves priority.

questions.question: How did you learn to manage your finances?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: My parents taught me caution, but I learned real management through work, spreadsheets and a few poor purchasing decisions. Mistakes are memorable teachers when they appear on a bank statement.
answers.alternative_a: I learned from budgeting apps and student life. A limited monthly allowance makes the relationship between choices and consequences very clear.
answers.alternative_b: I studied personal finance independently and created simple rules for saving and spending. Automation helped more than motivation.

questions.question: Is it harder for young people to save today?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, because housing, education and lifestyle costs have risen faster than many starting salaries. Young people also face constant advertising and social pressure to display a life that may not match their income.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. Rent takes a large share of income, and social life is expensive in cities. Saving requires more planning and sometimes living with family longer.
answers.alternative_b: In many cases, yes. Asset prices create a high entry barrier, although digital tools and financial education also give young people better information than previous generations had.

questions.question: Would you rather save or spend extra money?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: I would save most of it and spend a small part on something memorable. Complete self-denial is difficult to sustain, but spending every unexpected amount guarantees that larger goals remain unexpected too.
answers.alternative_a: I would divide it: half into savings, half into travel or a course. That way the money supports both future security and present experience.
answers.alternative_b: I would invest or save it unless there were a clear need. Extra money is valuable precisely because it can create options later.

questions.question: What is your usual means of transport?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I usually travel by motorbike because it is the fastest way to move through Ho Chi Minh City's dense traffic. It is practical for short journeys, although heat, rain and safety prevent me from calling it ideal.
answers.alternative_a: I use buses and walking for most university trips. The combination is affordable, and I can read or listen to music instead of concentrating on traffic.
answers.alternative_b: I mainly use a motorbike, with a car for family trips or bad weather. The motorbike remains more efficient for everyday distances.

questions.question: Why do you use it?
questions.quick_analysis: Give the main reason directly, explain the cause-and-effect link, and finish with a brief personal consequence.

answers.ta_refined: Speed and flexibility are the main reasons. I can leave when I choose, park near my destination and take smaller streets when major roads are congested.
answers.alternative_a: I use public transport because it is cheap and I do not need to find parking. The bus also gives me a predictable block of time to read.
answers.alternative_b: A motorbike suits local traffic and short distances. It costs less than driving and avoids the difficulty of parking a car in crowded areas.

questions.question: How long is your daily journey?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: Usually thirty to forty-five minutes each way, depending heavily on traffic and rain. The distance is not enormous, but city conditions can turn a routine journey into an unpredictable one.
answers.alternative_a: About forty minutes to campus. A direct route would be shorter, but the bus stops and walking add time.
answers.alternative_b: Roughly twenty-five minutes. Leaving ten minutes later can add another fifteen, so timing matters more than distance.

questions.question: Has transport in your city improved?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, there are better roads, ride-hailing services and plans for metro expansion. However, private vehicles still dominate, so improvement is visible without yet making daily travel genuinely easy.
answers.alternative_a: Public buses are cleaner and payment is becoming more convenient. The biggest change is better information through apps, which reduces uncertainty.
answers.alternative_b: Roads and bridges have improved, and some routes are faster. Traffic volume has also grown, so benefits are partly absorbed by demand.

questions.question: What form of transport would you like to use more?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: I would like to use the metro more once the network becomes practical. Reliable rail could turn travel time into reading time and reduce the stress of weather and traffic.
answers.alternative_a: I would cycle more if routes were safe and connected. It would combine transport with exercise and save money.
answers.alternative_b: I would like to use electric public transport more. Clean, frequent buses or rail would reduce both noise and dependence on private vehicles.

questions.question: Do you often use public transport?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not very often at present because my daily routes are easier by motorbike. I use buses or the metro when parking would be difficult or when I want to avoid driving, and I hope the network eventually becomes convenient enough for routine travel.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, almost every day. I take a bus to university and occasionally use the metro, so public transport shapes my timetable more than any other service.
