answers.alternative_b: Occasionally. I use buses for central areas where parking is inconvenient, but the routes do not cover every journey I make.

questions.question: What is the best thing about it?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: The best part is being able to use the travel time. I can read, reply to messages or simply look outside instead of negotiating traffic, which turns commuting from active stress into passive time.
answers.alternative_a: Affordability is the main advantage. A monthly pass costs far less than fuel, parking and ride-hailing, which matters greatly to students.
answers.alternative_b: It reduces the need for parking and allows more people to travel in less road space. For individual passengers, the freedom from driving is also valuable.

questions.question: What problems does public transport have in your city?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Coverage and frequency are still inconsistent. A trip that takes twenty minutes by motorbike may require several connections, and waiting in heat or rain makes the difference difficult to ignore.
answers.alternative_a: Buses can be crowded and delayed, especially at peak times. Some stops also lack shade or clear information.
answers.alternative_b: The network is fragmented. Routes work well in some corridors but do not connect residential areas efficiently, so the final part of a journey remains difficult.

questions.question: Did you use buses or trains as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I used buses occasionally for school trips, but everyday travel in my hometown was mainly by bicycle. Public transport felt like something used for longer journeys rather than daily life.
answers.alternative_a: I took the bus to secondary school for several years. It taught me punctuality because missing one meant waiting much longer than I wanted.
answers.alternative_b: Rarely. My childhood routes were short, and family motorbikes or bicycles were more common than buses.

questions.question: How could public transport be improved?
questions.quick_analysis: Identify the key factor or solution, explain how it works, and illustrate it with one practical consequence.

answers.ta_refined: It needs more frequent services, integrated payment and reliable real-time information. Comfortable stops and safe walking access also matter, because a good bus is not enough if reaching it is unpleasant.
answers.alternative_a: Dedicated bus lanes would improve punctuality, and student-friendly fares should remain. Clearer route maps would also help occasional users.
answers.alternative_b: The city should connect buses, rail and walking routes as one system. Frequency and last-mile access are more important than adding isolated showcase vehicles.

questions.question: Can you drive?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I can drive, although I use a motorbike more often in the city. A car is comfortable for family trips and bad weather, but in dense traffic it can feel like bringing a living room into a queue.
answers.alternative_a: I have a licence but do not own a car. I drive occasionally when my family travels, so I am confident on highways but less enthusiastic about narrow city parking.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, and I drive regularly. I learned in my early twenties and now use a car mainly for work and family journeys.

questions.question: How often do you travel by car?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: A few times a week, mostly with my family or when carrying equipment. For ordinary short trips, the motorbike is faster and far easier to park.
answers.alternative_a: Only once or twice a month. I usually travel by bus, but my parents let me drive on longer weekend trips.
answers.alternative_b: Almost daily, although I avoid the car for very short central journeys. It is useful for work, shopping and taking my parents places.

questions.question: What do you like or dislike about driving?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I like the privacy, air conditioning and ability to carry people safely. What I dislike is the amount of attention traffic demands; a comfortable seat does not make a ninety-minute jam relaxing.
answers.alternative_a: I enjoy the independence of driving, but parking makes me anxious. Finding a space can take longer than the final part of the journey.
answers.alternative_b: I like control over route and timing. I dislike congestion and the hidden maintenance tasks that continue even when the car seems fine.

questions.question: Are traffic jams common where you live?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Extremely common, especially during morning and evening peaks. A short delay, light rain or minor accident can quickly affect several roads because the network is already operating close to capacity.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, particularly around the city centre and school areas. I usually check traffic before agreeing to travel by car.
answers.alternative_b: They are common on major roads, although timing can avoid the worst periods. The problem is less severe than in Ho Chi Minh City but still growing.

questions.question: Would you like to own an electric car?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, once the charging network and battery costs become more practical. I like the quieter ride and lower local emissions, but I would not buy one merely to be an early adopter.
answers.alternative_a: I would, especially for city driving. The environmental benefit appeals to me, and lower running costs could offset the higher purchase price.
answers.alternative_b: Probably. An electric car suits short regular journeys, but I would compare battery durability, repair support and charging access very carefully.

questions.question: Do you enjoy travelling?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Very much. Travel removes me from familiar routines and gives ordinary activities - breakfast, walking, even getting lost - a fresh quality. I enjoy comfort, but the best trips usually include at least one unplanned moment.
answers.alternative_a: I love travelling because it gives me new food, photographs and stories. I become much more energetic when exploring a place than I am during a normal week.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, especially nature-focused trips. Travel helps me reset, although I prefer fewer well-planned journeys to constantly rushing from one destination to another.

questions.question: How often do you take trips?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: A few times a year, usually during school breaks or family holidays. Short domestic trips are easier to organise, while international travel requires more planning and a more persuasive conversation with the budget.
answers.alternative_a: I take short trips every couple of months and one longer holiday each year. Even a weekend away makes the semester feel less repetitive.
answers.alternative_b: Perhaps four or five times a year. Most are domestic trips involving the coast or mountains, with an occasional overseas journey.

questions.question: Do you prefer travelling alone or with others?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: With family or close friends. Shared travel creates stronger memories and practical support, although I also need moments alone during the trip; constant togetherness can test even excellent relationships.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer friends because we have similar energy and can change plans spontaneously. Solo travel interests me, but I have not yet become comfortable with it.
answers.alternative_b: One or two companions are ideal. I enjoy sharing transport and decisions, but large groups slow everything down and make compromise the main activity.

questions.question: What was the last place you visited?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: The last place I visited was Da Lat with my family. We enjoyed the cooler weather, walked around the lake and spent an unreasonable amount of time choosing cafes with mountain views.
answers.alternative_a: I recently went to Ninh Binh. The boat ride through limestone scenery was peaceful, and the landscape looked almost unreal in the morning mist.
answers.alternative_b: My last trip was to Hue. I explored the imperial sites, ate far too many local dishes and appreciated the slower rhythm of the city.

questions.question: Where would you like to travel next?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: Japan is high on my list because it combines efficient cities, natural scenery and a culture I have encountered through books and media. I would like enough time to move beyond Tokyo rather than treating the country as one large checklist.
answers.alternative_a: I want to visit Spain for the architecture, food and lively street culture. Barcelona and Seville would be my first choices.
answers.alternative_b: I would like to travel to New Zealand. The mountains and coast appeal to me, and a road trip there seems ideal for someone who prefers landscapes to shopping.

questions.question: What do you usually do during holidays?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I usually slow down, spend time with family and take at least one short trip. I still read or prepare a little work because completely switching off is difficult, but I try to make the days feel different from an ordinary weekend.
answers.alternative_a: I travel, meet friends and catch up on sleep. The first day is usually ambitious, and the second is often devoted to recovering from the first.
answers.alternative_b: I spend holidays outdoors, visit relatives and work on home projects. I prefer a loose structure so the time does not disappear into screens.

questions.question: Do you prefer active or relaxing holidays?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: A balance. I like exploring during the day, but I do not want every hour scheduled. One active morning followed by a slow afternoon feels more restorative than either extreme.
answers.alternative_a: Active holidays suit me. I want to walk, try food and see places, because staying beside a pool for a week would make me restless.
answers.alternative_b: Relaxing holidays, especially after a demanding work period. I still go outside, but I avoid turning rest into another performance target.

questions.question: Who do you normally travel with?
questions.quick_analysis: Make one clear choice first, then add a specific identifying detail and a short personal reason or reaction.

answers.ta_refined: Mostly with my wife and children. Family travel requires more bags, snacks and negotiation, but seeing a place through the children's reactions often makes familiar experiences feel new.
answers.alternative_a: I normally travel with two close friends. We know each other's habits well enough to avoid major conflict and still find surprises.
answers.alternative_b: I usually travel with family or one friend. Large groups are enjoyable for events but inefficient for longer journeys.

questions.question: What holiday did you enjoy as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I loved summer trips to the beach with my extended family. We stayed in simple accommodation, ate seafood and spent almost the entire day outside. The lack of luxury never felt like a limitation.
answers.alternative_a: My favourite childhood holiday was Tet because cousins gathered at my grandparents' house. The gifts were exciting, but the freedom to play together mattered more.
answers.alternative_b: I remember camping near a waterfall with my family. The equipment was basic and the night was uncomfortable, yet the adventure made it unforgettable.

questions.question: How do you plan a trip?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I begin with the purpose of the trip, then set a realistic budget and choose accommodation near the main activities. I plan essentials carefully but leave some free time, because a perfect spreadsheet can still produce a tiring holiday.
answers.alternative_a: I save places on a map, compare transport and read recent reviews. After that, I create a flexible daily list rather than a strict timetable.
answers.alternative_b: I plan around travel time, weather and one or two priorities per day. Overloading the itinerary is the fastest way to turn a holiday into logistics work.

questions.question: Are there many tourists in your hometown?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Quang Ngai receives tourists, although far fewer than major destinations like Da Nang or Hoi An. Visitors usually come for the coast, historical sites or nearby islands, so the tourism feels noticeable without overwhelming everyday life.
answers.alternative_a: Hai Phong attracts many domestic visitors, especially before trips to Cat Ba. The city itself is becoming more popular for food and architecture.
answers.alternative_b: The Mekong Delta receives a steady flow of visitors interested in rivers, markets and orchards. Some areas are busy, while smaller towns remain relatively quiet.

questions.question: What attractions do visitors usually see?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: They often visit My Khe Beach, Sa Huynh, Ly Son Island and historical sites connected to the region. The landscape is varied, but the attractions are spread out, so transport planning matters.
answers.alternative_a: Visitors see the colonial centre, food streets and nearby Cat Ba Island. Many are surprised that the city offers more than a transport stop.
answers.alternative_b: Floating markets, fruit gardens and river tours are the main attractions. Local food and homestays are also part of the experience.

questions.question: Does tourism benefit your area?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, it creates jobs, supports small businesses and gives local products a wider market. However, benefits need to be distributed carefully, or the area may gain revenue while residents absorb noise, waste and higher prices.
answers.alternative_a: Tourism benefits restaurants, transport and accommodation. It also encourages investment in public spaces, although seasonal dependence can make income unstable.
answers.alternative_b: It brings income to families and can preserve traditional activities when visitors value them. Poorly managed tourism, however, may turn genuine culture into a staged product.

questions.question: Is there a place in your country you recommend?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I would recommend the central coast, especially a route through Hue, Da Nang and Hoi An. The area combines history, beaches and excellent food within manageable travel distances.
answers.alternative_a: Ha Giang is my recommendation for dramatic mountain scenery and local culture. The roads demand care, but the views are extraordinary.
answers.alternative_b: Phong Nha is ideal for nature lovers. The caves, rivers and rural landscape feel adventurous without requiring international travel.

questions.question: Would you like to work in tourism?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: Possibly in tourism education or content, but not in front-line hospitality full-time. I enjoy sharing places and designing experiences, yet constant customer service during peak seasons would be demanding.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, perhaps in destination marketing. It would combine travel, storytelling and my degree, although the industry can be unstable.
answers.alternative_b: I would consider sustainable tourism planning. The technical and environmental side interests me more than hotel or tour operations.

questions.question: Are you good at reading maps?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Reasonably good. I can understand routes and orientation, but I still rotate a map occasionally, which some people consider a serious moral failure. Once I identify one landmark, the rest becomes much easier.
answers.alternative_a: I am decent with maps, especially digital ones. Paper maps take me longer because I am used to the reassuring blue dot.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, I am comfortable reading scale, direction and road patterns. I enjoy understanding the route rather than following instructions blindly.

questions.question: Do you use paper maps or digital maps?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Digital maps almost all the time because they show traffic, travel time and live location. A paper map is useful in remote areas, but in a city it cannot warn me that one road has become a parking lot.
answers.alternative_a: I use digital maps for daily life and save offline maps when travelling. Paper versions are attractive, but they are less practical on a crowded street.
answers.alternative_b: Digital maps for navigation, paper or static maps for planning. I like seeing the whole route before relying on turn-by-turn directions.

questions.question: Have you ever got lost?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, many times. The most memorable was in a foreign city where two streets had similar names. I walked confidently for twenty minutes before realising confidence had not improved the direction.
answers.alternative_a: I once got lost in an old neighbourhood after my phone battery died. Asking a shop owner was slightly embarrassing but led to a much better route.
answers.alternative_b: I have, usually while hiking or driving in unfamiliar areas. Getting lost is manageable when noticed early and much less amusing after sunset.

questions.question: Is it easy to give directions in English?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: It is manageable if I can use clear landmarks and simple steps. The difficulty is listening to my own explanation and realising halfway through that I have confused left and right.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, although I need phrases such as 'go past', 'turn at' and 'opposite'. Gestures still become part of the language when the route is complicated.
answers.alternative_b: Fairly easy. The key is limiting the number of instructions and confirming the destination instead of delivering a perfect but overwhelming route.

questions.question: Do you think people rely too much on navigation apps?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, in the sense that people often follow the screen without understanding the area. Navigation apps are extremely useful, but developing no mental map makes users helpless when the signal fails or the route is wrong.
answers.alternative_a: Probably. I have followed absurd shortcuts simply because the app sounded confident. People should still look at signs and surroundings.
answers.alternative_b: They do, but the solution is not abandoning the technology. Users should preview routes, notice landmarks and treat the app as advice rather than authority.

questions.question: Do you often stay in hotels?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: A few times a year, mainly during family trips or work events. I enjoy good hotels, but after several nights I begin to miss small things from home, particularly my own pillow and a kitchen that does not charge for water.
answers.alternative_a: Quite often for short trips and university events. I usually choose budget hotels or hostels because location matters more than luxury.
answers.alternative_b: Several times a year. My work occasionally requires travel, and I also use hotels on road trips when a rented apartment would be unnecessary.

questions.question: What makes accommodation comfortable?
questions.quick_analysis: Identify the key factor or solution, explain how it works, and illustrate it with one practical consequence.

answers.ta_refined: Cleanliness, a supportive bed, quiet air conditioning and reliable hot water matter most. Decorative cushions are welcome, but they cannot rescue a room where the basics fail.
answers.alternative_a: I need a clean room, natural light, good Wi-Fi and staff who communicate clearly. A central location can compensate for a smaller space.
answers.alternative_b: Comfort comes from sleep quality and practical design: soundproofing, useful sockets, strong water pressure and a desk that is actually usable.

questions.question: Do you prefer hotels or rented apartments?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: For a short stay, a hotel. Services and reception reduce effort. For a family trip of several days, a rented apartment gives us space, laundry and a kitchen, which can make the experience far easier.
answers.alternative_a: I prefer rented apartments because they feel local and allow more privacy. Hotels are better when I arrive late or need support.
answers.alternative_b: Hotels for business, apartments for longer leisure trips. The choice depends on whether convenience or living space matters more.

questions.question: Have you ever had a bad hotel experience?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I once stayed in a room beside a lift that announced every arrival through the night. The hotel was clean, but lack of sleep turned a minor design flaw into the defining feature of the trip.
answers.alternative_a: I had a booking disappear during a holiday weekend. The staff eventually found another room, but the uncertainty after a long journey was extremely stressful.
answers.alternative_b: A hotel once had unreliable hot water and poor soundproofing. Neither problem was dramatic alone, but together they made the stay exhausting.

questions.question: Would you like to work in a hotel?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: No, not as a long-term career. I respect hospitality work because it requires patience and emotional control, but dealing with complaints while remaining cheerful would drain me quickly.
answers.alternative_a: Possibly in marketing or events rather than reception. I like the creative side of hospitality but would find rotating shifts difficult.
answers.alternative_b: I would consider hotel technology or operations. Improving booking, energy use or guest systems interests me more than direct service.

questions.question: Do you enjoy celebrating birthdays?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, but I prefer warm, simple celebrations to large parties. A good meal with family and a few thoughtful messages feels meaningful; an elaborate event can make the birthday person strangely busy on their own day.
answers.alternative_a: I love birthdays. They give friends a reason to gather, take photos and make someone feel noticed, even if the celebration is not expensive.
answers.alternative_b: I enjoy them in moderation. I do not need a party every year, but I appreciate a clear pause to reflect and spend time with people I value.

questions.question: How did you celebrate your last birthday?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: My last birthday was a quiet family dinner at a restaurant I like. My children chose the cake, which meant the decoration was far more colourful than I would have selected, and that made it better.
answers.alternative_a: I had dinner with friends, then we went to a small live-music cafe. The plan was simple, but everyone stayed longer than expected.
answers.alternative_b: I took the day off, went for a coastal drive and had seafood with my family. It felt restful rather than ceremonial.

questions.question: Were birthdays more exciting when you were a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Definitely. As a child, the countdown began weeks in advance because cake, gifts and being the centre of attention felt extraordinary. Adult birthdays arrive faster and often compete with work schedules.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, childhood birthdays felt magical because each year seemed significant. Now the excitement comes more from seeing friends than from becoming older.
answers.alternative_b: They were more intense as a child. Today I value the day, but I do not wake up expecting life to change because the number has increased.

questions.question: What makes a good birthday gift?
questions.quick_analysis: Identify the key factor or solution, explain how it works, and illustrate it with one practical consequence.

answers.ta_refined: The best gift shows that the giver paid attention. It might be a book, an experience or something useful that solves a small problem. Price matters much less than the feeling of being accurately known.
answers.alternative_a: A personalised gift is ideal, especially one linked to a shared memory. It creates emotion that a generic expensive item may not.
answers.alternative_b: A good gift is useful, durable and suited to the person's interests. Surprise is pleasant, but relevance is more important.

questions.question: Are milestone birthdays important in your country?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, milestone birthdays are often celebrated more formally, especially the first birthday, eighteenth birthday or ages ending in zero. The significance varies by family, but people use them as natural points for gathering and reflection.
answers.alternative_a: They are becoming more important, partly because social media makes themed celebrations visible. Families also treat major ages as opportunities for professional photographs.
answers.alternative_b: Some are, particularly for children and older adults. The value is less the number itself than bringing relatives together at stages when life is changing.

questions.question: What is your favorite festival?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: Tet is my favourite because it combines family, food, memory and a genuine change in daily rhythm. The preparations can be exhausting, but the first quiet morning of the new year still feels different from an ordinary holiday.
answers.alternative_a: I love the Mid-Autumn Festival. Lanterns, mooncakes and children's activities make the evening colourful without requiring a long holiday.
answers.alternative_b: Tet is my favourite as well. It is the one festival that changes homes, streets and family routines across the whole country.

questions.question: How do people celebrate it?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Families clean and decorate their homes, prepare traditional food, visit relatives and give lucky money to children. Many people also visit temples or watch fireworks, so the celebration moves between private family rituals and public events.
answers.alternative_a: People buy lanterns and mooncakes, organise lion dances and take children out in the evening. Schools and neighbourhoods often hold small performances.
answers.alternative_b: During Tet, people travel home, honour ancestors, share meals and exchange good wishes. The days before the festival are almost as important as the holiday itself.

questions.question: Did you enjoy festivals as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Very much. Tet meant new clothes, lucky money, cousins and permission to eat more sweets than usual. I did not see the cleaning, cooking and travel stress that adults were managing behind the scenes.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, I loved carrying lanterns and watching lion dances. The streets felt transformed for one evening.
answers.alternative_b: Absolutely. Festivals made the year feel divided into memorable seasons, and family gatherings were larger because relatives lived closer.

questions.question: Do traditional festivals matter to young people?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, if traditions are allowed to evolve. Young people may not follow every ritual exactly, but festivals still provide identity, family connection and a pause from routine. Relevance disappears only when tradition is presented as obligation without meaning.
answers.alternative_a: They do. Even highly modern young people enjoy the food, clothes and social atmosphere, and many become more curious about origins as they grow older.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, although participation may look different. Digital greetings and travel have changed the form, but the need for shared cultural moments remains.

questions.question: Would you like to attend a festival abroad?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: I would like to attend Japan's cherry blossom festivals. The visual beauty is obvious, but I am also interested in the social ritual of gathering under the trees and appreciating something temporary.
answers.alternative_a: I want to experience Carnival in Brazil. The music, costumes and street energy seem completely different from the festivals I know.
answers.alternative_b: Oktoberfest in Germany would be interesting, not only for the food and drink but also for observing how a regional tradition became a global event.

questions.question: Do you enjoy attending weddings?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, when I know the couple well. Weddings bring people together and carry a sense of occasion that ordinary gatherings lack. The less enjoyable part is attending as a distant acquaintance and trying to remember which side of the family I belong to.
answers.alternative_a: I enjoy them because everyone makes an effort with clothes, photos and speeches. They can be tiring, but the atmosphere is usually warm.
answers.alternative_b: Generally yes. I like the ceremony and family reunion, although very large weddings can feel more like event management than celebration.

questions.question: What usually happens at a wedding in your country?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: There is usually a ceremony followed by a large meal with relatives, friends and colleagues. Guests give money in envelopes, the couple visits tables and photographs happen continuously, often before anyone has eaten properly.
answers.alternative_a: Vietnamese weddings often include family rituals, formal photographs and a banquet. Music, speeches and table visits keep the event lively.
answers.alternative_b: The exact customs vary by region, but family introductions, ancestral respect and a shared meal are central. Modern venues have added screens, staged entrances and detailed programmes.

questions.question: Have celebrations become more expensive?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Definitely. Venues, decoration, photography and guest expectations have all become more elaborate. Social media may intensify the pressure because couples compare their event with highly polished images rather than ordinary reality.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, even modest celebrations can become costly once clothing, gifts and professional services are included. Some couples now choose smaller events to protect their finances.
answers.alternative_b: They have, partly because weddings have become packaged experiences. Greater choice is positive, but it can turn personal meaning into a competition of production value.

questions.question: Do you prefer large or small celebrations?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Small celebrations. With fewer guests, the couple can speak to everyone and the atmosphere feels personal. A huge wedding may look impressive while leaving the hosts too busy to enjoy it.
answers.alternative_a: I like medium-sized celebrations. I want energy and a full room, but not so many people that half the guests are strangers to the couple.
answers.alternative_b: Small and well organised. Meaningful interaction matters more to me than scale, and logistics become much easier.

questions.question: What celebration would you like to organize?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I would like to organise a family anniversary on the coast, with a simple outdoor dinner and photographs across several generations. The goal would be to create time together rather than a highly scripted performance.
answers.alternative_a: I would organise a surprise graduation party for close friends, with a photo wall and short video messages from people who could not attend.
answers.alternative_b: I would plan a small community sports day. It would be active, inclusive and easier to remember than another formal banquet.

questions.question: Is it important to be on time?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, because punctuality shows respect for other people's time and keeps plans from creating unnecessary stress. I do not think a two-minute delay is a moral failure, but habitual lateness sends a fairly clear message.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. Being on time makes group activities smoother, and I feel uncomfortable when others are waiting because of me.
answers.alternative_b: It is important, especially in professional situations. Reliability begins with small promises such as arriving when agreed.

questions.question: Are you usually punctual?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Usually, yes. I build in extra travel time because Ho Chi Minh City traffic is too unpredictable for optimistic planning. I still arrive late occasionally, but it is normally despite preparation rather than because I started getting ready at the meeting time.
answers.alternative_a: I am punctual for classes and appointments, although social events are a little more flexible. I would rather wait ten minutes than enter a room apologising.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, almost obsessively. I check routes and prepare things the night before, which reduces the number of excuses available in the morning.

questions.question: What kinds of appointments must never be missed?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: Medical appointments, flights, examinations and job interviews must never be missed. In those situations, lateness can affect health, money or another person's assessment, so the consequences extend beyond mild inconvenience.
answers.alternative_a: Exams and interviews are the most serious because late arrival can close the opportunity entirely. Important family ceremonies also deserve careful timing.
answers.alternative_b: Flights, court or official appointments and critical work meetings require absolute punctuality. The cost of failure is too high to rely on a last-minute journey.

questions.question: Have you ever been late for something important?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I was once late for an important meeting because a minor accident blocked the road. I had left early, but not early enough for that level of disruption, and the experience permanently changed how much buffer time I allow.
answers.alternative_a: I arrived late for a university presentation after getting on the wrong bus. My group covered the opening, but I felt guilty and checked every route twice afterwards.
answers.alternative_b: I nearly missed a flight because I underestimated airport traffic. I made it, but running through a terminal with luggage is a poor way to begin a holiday.

questions.question: Do people in your country tend to be punctual?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: It depends on the setting. People are generally punctual for work, travel and official appointments, but social gatherings often begin later than the stated time. The phrase 'Vietnamese time' is sometimes used jokingly, although attitudes are becoming stricter.
answers.alternative_a: Formal situations are usually respected, while parties and weddings may start late because guests expect flexibility. Younger professionals seem increasingly time-conscious.
answers.alternative_b: There is a clear difference between business and social life. People value punctuality, but cultural tolerance for delay remains higher at informal events.

questions.question: Would you describe yourself as patient?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: More patient than I used to be, especially with students and children. Teaching has shown me that repeating an explanation calmly often works better than showing frustration, although traffic can still reveal that my progress is incomplete.
answers.alternative_a: I am patient with people but less patient with slow technology. I can listen to a friend for an hour, yet a frozen laptop tests my character within thirty seconds.
answers.alternative_b: Generally yes. I like understanding a problem before reacting, but repeated carelessness can exhaust my patience quickly.

questions.question: What situations test your patience?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Long queues, avoidable delays and people who speak loudly on their phones test me most. Waiting itself is manageable; feeling that the delay could easily have been prevented is much harder.
answers.alternative_a: Group projects test my patience, especially when someone disappears until the final day and returns with strong opinions.
answers.alternative_b: Unclear processes and repeated meetings are difficult. I can tolerate complex work, but unnecessary inefficiency frustrates me.

questions.question: Were you more impatient as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Definitely. As a child, I wanted results immediately and found waiting almost physically painful. Age has taught me that many worthwhile things - skills, savings and relationships - move slowly whether I approve or not.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, I was easily frustrated when games or homework became difficult. Now I can step away and return instead of treating one obstacle as a personal insult.
answers.alternative_b: I was more impatient and competitive. Experience has made me better at separating temporary delay from actual failure.

questions.question: How do you stay calm while waiting?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I usually read, listen to something or break the wait into a useful task. If nothing can be done, slow breathing helps more than repeatedly checking the time, although I still check it occasionally.
answers.alternative_a: I bring earphones and a book almost everywhere. Turning waiting into listening or reading makes it feel less stolen.
answers.alternative_b: I focus on what I can control, such as planning the next step or observing the situation. Anger rarely shortens the queue.

questions.question: Is patience an important quality at work or school?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Absolutely. Learning and work both involve mistakes, delayed results and cooperation with different personalities. Patience keeps people engaged long enough to improve, whereas frustration often damages the very process it wants to speed up.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially in group work and skill development. Students who expect instant mastery may give up before real progress begins.
answers.alternative_b: It is essential, but it should not mean passivity. Good professionals remain calm while still addressing repeated problems clearly.

questions.question: Do you often feel bored?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not often, mainly because there is always something to read, improve or organise. I do feel bored during long passive waits, but even then my mind usually begins planning a lesson or creating a problem that did not previously exist.
answers.alternative_a: Sometimes, especially during repetitive lectures or quiet weekends. My phone makes boredom easy to escape, although not always in a satisfying way.
answers.alternative_b: Rarely. I enjoy being alone and can usually find a project, but compulsory social events with no clear purpose can feel very slow.

questions.question: What kinds of situations bore you?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: Repetitive meetings bore me, particularly when everyone is restating information that could have been written in five lines. I also struggle with entertainment that is loud but has no real story.
answers.alternative_a: Long queues and conversations that never move beyond gossip bore me. I need either a genuine connection or something new to think about.
answers.alternative_b: Passive waiting and highly predictable films are difficult. I can handle repetition when it serves a goal, but not when it is simply poor planning.

questions.question: What do you do to make time pass more quickly?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I read, listen to a podcast or turn the time into a small task. If I am with other people, I ask a more interesting question rather than waiting for the conversation to improve by itself.
answers.alternative_a: I take photos, message a friend or make a list. Sometimes I deliberately do nothing for a few minutes because constant stimulation is exhausting too.
answers.alternative_b: I walk, organise files or solve a short puzzle. Physical movement is especially effective when boredom comes from sitting too long.

questions.question: Were you easily bored as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: No, I was good at inventing games with friends and could stay occupied with very little. A cardboard box had more entertainment value than many expensive toys because we decided what it was.
answers.alternative_a: I was easily bored when adults were talking, but rarely when I was with other children. Imagination filled most empty time.
answers.alternative_b: I became bored during long family visits, so I carried books or found mechanical objects to examine. The habit of making my own activity began early.

questions.question: Can boredom ever be useful?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, in small doses. Boredom can create the empty mental space where ideas appear, and it reveals which activities people choose without external pressure. The problem is that phones now remove boredom before it has time to become useful.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. Some of my best ideas come after the first uncomfortable minutes of having nothing planned. Boredom encourages creativity if people do not escape immediately.
answers.alternative_b: It can be useful as a signal. Repeated boredom may show that a routine needs challenge or meaning, although prolonged boredom can also harm motivation.

questions.question: Do you often remember your dreams?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Typically not. I may remember a few strange fragments when I wake up, but they fade almost immediately. Most of them make so little sense that forgetting is probably the brain's most efficient editing decision.
answers.alternative_a: I remember dreams quite often, especially vivid ones near morning. I sometimes write a line in my phone before the details disappear.
answers.alternative_b: Only occasionally. Stressful or unusual dreams stay, while ordinary ones vanish before breakfast.

questions.question: What kinds of dreams do you have?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: They are usually disorganised combinations of work, travel and people from different periods of my life. A normal classroom can suddenly become an airport, and nobody in the dream considers this unusual.
answers.alternative_a: I often dream about being late, getting lost or returning to school. The situations are stressful but also strangely repetitive.
answers.alternative_b: My dreams tend to involve problem-solving or places I have recently visited. They borrow real details and rearrange them without concern for logic.

questions.question: Do you ever talk about dreams with other people?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Sometimes with my wife, especially if the dream was funny or involved someone we know. I do not analyse every detail; it is more like sharing a bizarre story created overnight.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, with close friends. Comparing dreams can be entertaining because everyone accepts impossible events without needing an explanation.
answers.alternative_b: Rarely. Unless a dream is unusually vivid, describing it often sounds far less interesting than experiencing it.

questions.question: Did you have a recurring dream as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, I repeatedly dreamed that I had forgotten an exam until the final minutes. The setting changed, but the panic remained. Apparently school pressure continued working night shifts long after the day ended.
answers.alternative_a: I used to dream about flying over my neighbourhood. It felt so real that waking up was always slightly disappointing.
answers.alternative_b: I often dreamed that I was lost in a huge building. I never reached the destination, which was frustrating even in sleep.

questions.question: Do you think dreams have meanings?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: They may reflect emotions, recent experiences or worries, but I am sceptical of fixed symbolic interpretations. A dream about water could mean stress, memory or simply that it rained all night.
answers.alternative_a: I think they can reveal what the mind is processing, although not in a simple dictionary-like way. Personal context matters more than universal symbols.
answers.alternative_b: Some meaning is possible, especially emotional patterns, but dreams are also products of memory and biology. I would not base a major decision on one.

questions.question: How many hours do you usually sleep?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: I aim for seven hours, though the real number is often closer to six and a half. I function on that, but the difference between functioning and feeling genuinely rested becomes clearer with age.
answers.alternative_a: About seven to eight hours. I need more during exam periods because mental tiredness seems to accumulate even when I am sitting most of the day.
answers.alternative_b: Usually seven hours. I keep a regular schedule because inconsistent sleep affects my concentration and training very quickly.

questions.question: Do you sleep well?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Most nights, yes. I fall asleep fairly easily if I stop working at a sensible time. The problem is that 'one last small task' has a habit of becoming an hour.
answers.alternative_a: Not always. I sleep well once I am asleep, but I sometimes stay awake thinking about deadlines or replaying conversations.
answers.alternative_b: Generally well. A cool room, exercise and limited caffeine help, although travel can disrupt my routine.

questions.question: Do you ever take naps?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Occasionally at weekends. A twenty-minute nap can be refreshing, but a long afternoon sleep leaves me confused about the time and makes bedtime much harder.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, especially after early classes. I set an alarm for thirty minutes because an unplanned nap can consume the entire afternoon.
answers.alternative_b: Rarely. Naps usually make me groggy, so I prefer a short walk or coffee if energy drops.

questions.question: Did you sleep more when you were younger?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: In total, probably yes. As a teenager, I slept late and could remain in bed for hours at weekends. Now responsibilities start earlier, and my body seems less willing to recover from poor choices.
answers.alternative_a: I slept longer as a child because my schedule was simpler and adults enforced bedtime. University offers more freedom and less wisdom.
answers.alternative_b: I slept more irregularly when younger, not necessarily more. I now protect a consistent seven hours instead of alternating between very short and very long nights.

questions.question: What helps you fall asleep?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Reading a paper book, dimming the lights and keeping my phone away from the bed all help. Calm instrumental music also works, provided I do not use the device to find a better playlist for forty minutes.
answers.alternative_a: A warm shower and writing tomorrow's tasks help me. Once worries are on paper, my mind stops trying to repeat them.
answers.alternative_b: Exercise, a cool room and no caffeine after lunch are the main factors. I also use a simple breathing routine when work thoughts continue.

questions.question: What do you do to stay healthy?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: I exercise three times a week, eat a reasonably balanced diet and try to protect my sleep. None of this is perfect, but the consistency matters more than occasional bursts of extreme discipline.
answers.alternative_a: I walk a lot, cook most meals and attend a dance class. I also try to manage stress because physical habits are much harder when my schedule feels chaotic.
answers.alternative_b: I combine strength training, badminton and regular meals. Annual health checks and basic preventive habits matter to me as much as visible fitness.

questions.question: Do you think you have a healthy lifestyle?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Mostly, yes. I am active and pay attention to food, but I sit for long periods and sometimes work too late. I would call the lifestyle healthy with several honest footnotes.
answers.alternative_a: Fairly healthy. I move often and rarely smoke or drink, although my sleep becomes irregular during exams.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, by practical standards. I exercise, limit processed food and monitor key health indicators, but I do not treat health as a competition.

questions.question: How often do you have a medical check-up?
questions.quick_analysis: State the frequency, amount or duration clearly, then qualify it with a normal situation and one realistic exception.

answers.ta_refined: Once a year for a general check-up, unless a specific issue appears. Preventive checks are easy to postpone when I feel fine, so I schedule them like any other important appointment.
answers.alternative_a: Every one or two years. I know annual checks would be better, but students often respond to symptoms rather than calendars.
answers.alternative_b: Annually, with extra tests when advised. Family history makes regular monitoring a sensible investment.

questions.question: What unhealthy habit would you like to change?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I would like to stop working late at night. The extra hour often produces lower-quality work and steals energy from the next day, but unfinished tasks can still feel more urgent than invisible fatigue.
answers.alternative_a: I want to reduce sugary drinks. They are easy during busy days, but the habit adds cost and leaves me tired later.
answers.alternative_b: I would spend less uninterrupted time sitting. Even with regular exercise, eight hours at a desk is not something one gym session can fully cancel.

questions.question: Has health become more important to you with age?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer the experience or change directly, give one specific before-and-after detail, and explain why it matters.

answers.ta_refined: Definitely. In my twenties, health felt automatic and distant. Now sleep, posture and diet produce immediate consequences, so taking care of myself feels less like prevention and more like daily maintenance.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, because I have seen stress affect friends and family. I think more about long-term habits than appearance now.
answers.alternative_b: It has. Recovery is slower, responsibilities are greater and health supports every other goal. Age has made the connection more concrete.

questions.question: Is your home area noisy?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: The alley itself is quiet, but the surrounding district is not. During peak hours I hear traffic, construction and the occasional loudspeaker, so the house feels like a small pocket of calm inside a very energetic city.
answers.alternative_a: Yes, my area is busy because of students, cafes and traffic. It becomes quieter after midnight, which is not especially helpful when I need to sleep earlier.
answers.alternative_b: My street is fairly quiet, apart from morning market activity and occasional construction. The coastal wind is often more noticeable than traffic.

questions.question: What kinds of sounds do you enjoy?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: I enjoy birds, rain and the low background sound of a cafe. Complete silence can feel sterile, while gentle natural or social sounds create atmosphere without demanding attention.
answers.alternative_a: I like acoustic music, conversation from a distance and the sound of rain on a window. They make a space feel alive.
answers.alternative_b: Sea waves, wind in trees and mechanical sounds that are steady rather than sudden all appeal to me.

questions.question: What noise do you find annoying?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Drilling and repetitive construction noise are the worst because they enter the body as much as the ears. Loud karaoke late at night is a close second, especially when enthusiasm exceeds musical accuracy.
answers.alternative_a: Motorbike horns annoy me, particularly when they are used continuously rather than as warnings. The sound creates stress without improving movement.
answers.alternative_b: Sudden alarms, modified exhausts and loud phone videos in public spaces bother me most. They force one person's choice onto everyone nearby.

questions.question: Do you need silence when studying or working?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: I need relative quiet for writing and complex planning. Soft instrumental music is fine, but lyrics compete with language in my head. For routine tasks, a little background noise actually helps.
answers.alternative_a: I study best with low cafe noise or instrumental music. Complete silence makes every small sound noticeable.
answers.alternative_b: For coding, I prefer quiet or predictable background sound. Conversations are distracting because my attention automatically follows them.

questions.question: Have cities become noisier?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, as traffic, construction and dense living have increased. Technology has also added personal noise through speakers and devices, so public space contains more overlapping sound than before.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. Cities operate later, and delivery vehicles, entertainment and construction extend the noisy part of the day.
answers.alternative_b: They have become noisier, although better building design and electric transport could reduce some sources. Urban growth has outpaced acoustic planning.

questions.question: Do you like crowded places?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not really. I can tolerate a lively market or event for a while, but dense crowds make movement and conversation tiring. I enjoy atmosphere; I do not enjoy becoming part of a slow human traffic jam.
answers.alternative_a: Sometimes. Crowds at festivals or concerts create excitement, but crowded transport and shopping centres feel completely different.
answers.alternative_b: I generally avoid them. I prefer places where I can move freely and understand what is happening around me.

questions.question: When was the last time you were somewhere crowded?
questions.quick_analysis: Anchor the answer in a clear time, add one vivid detail, and connect the memory to how you see it now.

answers.ta_refined: The last truly crowded place was a shopping centre before Tet. Every family seemed to be buying gifts at the same time, and finding a table for dinner required more strategy than the shopping itself.
answers.alternative_a: I was at a weekend music festival recently. The crowd was huge, but the shared energy made it enjoyable rather than stressful.
answers.alternative_b: A night market during a holiday was the last example. It was interesting for an hour, then the noise and slow movement became exhausting.

questions.question: What crowded place is common in your city?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Traditional markets, shopping centres and major intersections are often crowded. During festivals, walking streets and public squares become especially dense because everyone wants the same photograph from the same place.
answers.alternative_a: The old quarter and popular lakes are crowded at weekends. Bus stations become extremely busy before holidays.
answers.alternative_b: Beaches, bridges and night markets attract large crowds during weekends and festivals, especially in the summer tourist season.

questions.question: How do you feel in a large crowd?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: Initially alert, then tired. I become more conscious of bags, children and exit routes, so even a cheerful crowd demands mental energy. If the space is well organised, I can relax much more.
answers.alternative_a: I feel excited when the crowd has a clear purpose, such as a concert. In an unstructured crush, I become anxious and want more space.
answers.alternative_b: I feel uncomfortable and less in control. I tend to move towards the edge, where I can see routes and breathe more easily.

questions.question: Do you think public places are becoming more crowded?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, because urban populations, tourism and commercial events are growing faster than public space. Social media also concentrates people in a small number of fashionable locations instead of distributing them across the city.
answers.alternative_a: They seem to be, especially on weekends. Better transport brings more people to the same centres, while public spaces have not expanded equally.
answers.alternative_b: In popular areas, yes. The issue is not only population but design; poor entrances and narrow walkways can make moderate numbers feel overwhelming.

questions.question: Do you often help other people?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, mostly in small practical ways. I help students understand difficult work, assist neighbours with information and support family members when they need time or transport. Help is often ordinary rather than heroic.
answers.alternative_a: Quite often. I share notes, help classmates prepare presentations and volunteer at occasional university events.
answers.alternative_b: Yes, when I have the relevant skill or time. I prefer useful assistance to dramatic offers that create more coordination than value.

questions.question: What kind of help do you usually give?
questions.quick_analysis: Name one main preference, narrow it with a concrete example, and explain the personal appeal instead of listing many options.

answers.ta_refined: My help is usually educational or technical. I explain English, review documents, solve computer problems and occasionally help someone organise a plan that has become too complicated.
answers.alternative_a: I help friends with study, photography and event organisation. I am also the person people ask to write a careful message.
answers.alternative_b: I troubleshoot devices, give rides and help with physical tasks. Practical problems are easier for me to respond to than vague emotional requests.

questions.question: Did your parents encourage you to help others?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes. My parents expected us to share household work and help older relatives without treating it as a special performance. Their message was simple: if you can reduce someone's burden, do it.
answers.alternative_a: They did, especially through visiting relatives and donating useful items. I learned that help should respect what people actually need.
answers.alternative_b: Yes. My father often fixed things for neighbours, and I saw that community trust grows through repeated small actions.

questions.question: When did someone last help you?
questions.quick_analysis: Anchor the answer in a clear time, add one vivid detail, and connect the memory to how you see it now.

answers.ta_refined: A colleague recently covered a class when a family issue appeared unexpectedly. The practical help mattered, but what I remember most is that they offered before I had to explain or negotiate.
answers.alternative_a: A friend helped me rehearse for an interview last week. She listened to the same answer several times and still found constructive things to say.
answers.alternative_b: My neighbour helped jump-start my motorbike battery. It took ten minutes, but it saved a much larger disruption.

questions.question: Should schools teach children to do community work?
questions.quick_analysis: State a clear opinion, support it with one reason, and add a qualification so the answer sounds balanced rather than absolute.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, provided the work is meaningful and age-appropriate. Community projects can teach responsibility and empathy, but students should understand the issue rather than simply collect a certificate or pose for photographs.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. Service activities connect lessons with real people and help students see that contribution is a normal part of citizenship.
answers.alternative_b: Schools should, but quality matters. A small sustained project is better than one compulsory day that creates more work for the organisation being helped.

questions.question: Do you often lose things?
questions.quick_analysis: Give a confident yes, no or qualified answer, then support it with one focused reason and a brief real-life detail.

answers.ta_refined: Not often, mainly because I keep keys, wallet and phone in fixed places. When I do lose something, it is usually because I temporarily ignored the system and placed it somewhere 'safe', which is often another word for invisible.
answers.alternative_a: I misplace small items fairly often, especially when I am rushing. I usually find them, but not before accusing the universe of moving them.
answers.alternative_b: Rarely. I have developed routines for important objects, although tools occasionally disappear during a project.

questions.question: What item do you lose most frequently?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer with one central idea, develop it through a specific example, and finish with a genuine reaction or small twist.

answers.ta_refined: Pens are the item I lose most frequently. They move between classrooms, bags and desks, and apparently some begin independent lives with students.
answers.alternative_a: Hair ties and earphones disappear constantly. They are small enough to hide in every pocket except the one I check.
answers.alternative_b: Small charging cables are the main problem. I own several, yet the correct one is rarely where I expect it.

questions.question: How do you usually find something you have misplaced?
questions.quick_analysis: Answer directly, develop one focused idea with a concrete detail, and close in a way that reveals personality.

answers.ta_refined: I stop moving, reconstruct the last few actions and search one area at a time. Random panic makes me check the same place repeatedly, so a calm sequence is much faster, even if calm is not my first reaction.
answers.alternative_a: I call or message the device if possible, then empty my bag completely. Asking another person to look helps because they do not share my assumptions.
answers.alternative_b: I retrace my route and check transition points such as doors, tables and vehicles. Important devices also have tracking enabled.

questions.question: Did you lose things more often as a child?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a past-time marker, describe one concrete memory, and close with a present-day reflection or contrast.

answers.ta_refined: Yes, because I moved constantly and treated possessions casually. School items vanished into classrooms, friends' houses and mysterious corners of my own room.
answers.alternative_a: Definitely. I lost pencils, toys and at least one school hat every year. My parents eventually labelled everything with my name.
answers.alternative_b: A little more. I had fewer systems and often left sports equipment wherever the game ended.

questions.question: What would you do if you found someone else’s valuable item?
questions.quick_analysis: Use a natural hypothetical form, choose one realistic idea, and make it memorable with a concrete result or image.

answers.ta_refined: I would try to identify the owner, hand it to staff or police if appropriate and keep a clear record of where it was found. A valuable item can carry personal data as well as money, so returning it securely matters.
answers.alternative_a: I would look for contact details and give it to the management of the place. I would not post sensitive information publicly just to prove I found it.
answers.alternative_b: I would secure it, document the location and contact the relevant authority. Keeping it would be both unethical and likely traceable.
